Leconte de Lisle (22 October 1818 – 17 July 1894) was a French poet. His full name was Charles Marie René Leconte de Lisle. He was born in Saint-Paul, on the island of Bourbon. The island is now called Réunion. It is a French island in the Indian Ocean, east of Africa. Leconte de Lisle was the leader of a group of French poets called the Parnassians (in French, les Parnassiens). They believed that a poem should be a perfect and beautiful work of art. They wrote their poems slowly and carefully. They also believed that poets should not write about their own private feelings. For this reason, people often called Leconte de Lisle "impassive", which means "showing no emotion". However, his poems often express strong feelings. He hides these feelings in pictures of gods, animals, and lands far away. He wrote three main books of poems: Poèmes antiques (Ancient Poems, 1852), Poèmes barbares (Barbarian Poems, 1862), and Poèmes tragiques (Tragic Poems, 1884). He also translated Homer and other poets from Ancient Greece into French prose. In 1886, he became a member of the Académie française, a famous group of French writers. He took the place that had belonged to Victor Hugo, one of the most famous French writers of the time. Leconte de Lisle had a difficult life. He was poor for many years. In 1848, he publicly supported the end of slavery. This caused a serious break between him and his family. He supported the republic, a form of government without a king. He was not religious, and he opposed the political power of the Church. Many younger poets learned from his work. They included Sully Prudhomme, the first person to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, José-Maria de Heredia, Paul Verlaine, and Stéphane Mallarmé. The name "Leconte de Lisle" looks like the name of a noble family. It is not. The poet's family were town people from the border of Normandy and Brittany, in the west of France. For many generations they were apothecaries, who prepared and sold medicines, and doctors. The family name was "Le Conte". Around 1712 one of them married the daughter of a man who owned a small piece of land called "l'Isle". Owning this land did not give the family a noble title. In old France, families often added the name of a piece of land to their own name, to tell brothers and cousins apart. In this way the words "de Lisle" came into the family. The poet himself was the first to write "Le" and "Conte" as one word. He said he did this so that his name would not look like a title of nobility. The poet's father was born in Dinan, in Brittany, and studied medicine. In 1813, he became an army surgeon, a doctor who performs operations, in the armies of Napoleon. After the wars ended, he sailed to Bourbon Island. In 1817, he married Élysée de Riscourt de Lanux. She was a "Creole". At that time, people in the colonies used this word for a person from a European family who had been born in the colony. Her family had lived on the island since 1720. It was related to Évariste de Parny (1753–1814), a poet from Bourbon who was famous around 1800. The couple owned a plantation, or very large farm, in the hills above Saint-Paul. They grew sugar cane there, and enslaved people did the work. Their first child, Charles, was born on 22 October 1818. They later had two more sons and three daughters. In a short text about his life, the poet wrote that he came to France when he was three years old. He returned to Bourbon with his family when he was about ten. During his years in France, he went to school in Nantes. After he returned to the island, he grew up between the mountains and the sea. The powerful landscape remained in his memory for the rest of his life. He did not like school, but he loved reading. One day, the head of his school in Saint-Denis, the capital of the island, told his mother that he had not been to class for a week. The boy admitted that he had gone to the town library instead. He had spent each day there reading the novels of Walter Scott. His mother did not punish him. She bought him the novels and asked him to read them at home. Later, he discovered Les Orientales (1829), a book of poems by Victor Hugo. The book had a strong effect on him. In a speech given fifty years later, he said that these poems had shown him the full beauty of his island for the first time. He began to write poems when he was a teenager. His first political ideas came from his father's books. His father admired the free thinkers of the eighteenth century, who wanted people to use reason instead of simply accepting religious or political ideas. Leconte de Lisle also fell in love with a young cousin from the Lanux family, although he only saw her from far away. Every Sunday, she came down to the church in Saint-Paul in a "manchy". This was a light chair with a cover, carried by enslaved people. She died when she was very young, and he never forgot her. Many years later, he described her in one of his most gentle poems, Le Manchy (1862): Sous un nuage frais de claire mousseline, Par les rampes de la colline... (Literal English translation: "Under a fresh cloud of light muslin, every Sunday morning, you came to town in a rattan manchy, down the slopes of the hill...") His family wanted him to become a magistrate, or judge. To do this, he had to study law in France. On 11 March 1837, he left Bourbon by ship and sailed to Nantes. The journey lasted more than three months. Some old books say that he also travelled to India and Java when he was young. This story is not true. His letters show that the journey to France was his first long voyage. The ship stopped at the Cape of Good Hope. There, he saw a stuffed panther, lions in cages, and wild dogs howling at the sea. These animals later appeared in his poems. The ship also stopped at Saint Helena, where he visited the grave of Napoleon. In a letter, he wrote that the emperor was only a tyrant. Because Napoleon had been more powerful than other tyrants, Leconte de Lisle thought that he was also more guilty. In Brittany, he lived with a strict uncle in Dinan. His uncle often wrote to the family in Bourbon to complain about him. On 14 November 1838, Leconte de Lisle passed the baccalauréat, the French examination taken at the end of secondary school, in Rennes. He received a poor mark in Greek. This was surprising because he later became a translator of Homer. He soon gave up his law studies. In 1840 and 1841, he was the main writer for a small literary magazine in Rennes called La Variété. He published poems and articles in it. His family became tired of his behaviour. At the end of 1839, they stopped sending him money for some time. Several difficult years followed. At the end of 1842, he tried to start a newspaper called Le Scorpion. It was a satirical newspaper, which meant that it used humour to attack people and ideas. The printer refused to print it, and Leconte de Lisle lost a court case about the newspaper in January 1843. In October 1843, he sailed back to Bourbon. He had not received a law degree, but he was now certain that he wanted to be a writer. The two years at home were unhappy. He worked in Saint-Denis as a business agent and hated it. In his letters he judged the planter society around him very hard, and he suffered when he saw how the masters treated their slaves. His relatives laughed at "the poet". In a famous letter of this time he wrote that he was pulling away from single persons and learning to think about humanity as a whole: "I erase myself, I make myself a synthesis." These strange words already announce the impersonal poet. A door opened in 1845. A newspaper in Paris, La Démocratie pacifique, offered him a small salary and the printing of a book of poems. On 23 March 1845 he sailed for France on the ship Anna. He never saw his island again. La Démocratie pacifique was the daily newspaper of the Fourierists, the followers of the thinker Charles Fourier (1772–1837). Fourier had dreamed of a perfect society organized in large communities; such a dream of a perfect society is called a "utopia". Leconte de Lisle wrote for the newspaper and for its monthly review, La Phalange, from 1845 to 1848. He shared the great hopes of the school: justice for the poor and the end of oppression. He earned one hundred and fifty francs a month. When the newspaper had no money, the young editors met in the evening around glasses of sugared water and talked about the liberation of the world. The scholar Caroline De Mulder has shown that this socialist period was not a small accident. The ideas of justice, and the fight against the power of the Church, stayed present in his work to the end. In Paris he also discovered Greece. Two young scholars, Louis Ménard and Thalès Bernard, became his friends and guided his reading. Through them he met the poets Charles Baudelaire and Théodore de Banville. Like many educated Europeans of that time, he came to see the art of Ancient Greece as calm, simple, and perfect. In 1846 he published verses about the Venus de Milo, the famous Greek statue of the Louvre museum, and in 1846 and 1847 he wrote his first Greek poems, such as Hypatie and Niobé. Most of them entered his first great book in 1852. In February 1848 a revolution broke out in Paris. The king ran away, and France became a republic (see Revolutions of 1848). The new government prepared a law to free the slaves in the French colonies. When the planters protested, Leconte de Lisle called together the young Creoles of Paris. He carried to the town hall a public letter in which they welcomed the end of slavery as an act of justice. On 27 April 1848 the government signed the decree, and slavery was abolished in the French colonies. His support for abolition angered his family, whose income came partly from plantations worked by enslaved people. His father, who had begun to help him again, now stopped sending him money for good. This made an already difficult situation worse. The poet also worked for the revolution itself: a Paris club sent him to Brittany to campaign for the republican candidates. The mission failed. In Dinan, after a speech against the Church, a crowd wanted to stone him, and he escaped through a window. In June 1848, when the army crushed the revolt of the Paris workers, he was arrested and spent, he said later, two days and two nights in prison. The year 1848 changed him deeply. He kept his republican faith until his death, but he stopped believing that politics could quickly change the world. In a letter of 1849 he wrote that the works of Homer count for more in the moral history of humanity than political pamphlets. From this time he gave his life to poetry. For almost ten years he lived in deep poverty in a small room in the rue Cassette in Paris, giving private lessons in Greek and Latin. His first book was born almost by accident. A bookshop owner, Marc Ducloux, had lost a manuscript that the poet sold him. To repair the mistake, he offered to print a book of his poems. So, at the end of November 1852, the Poèmes antiques appeared. The book sold very few copies, but several important critics noticed it: Sainte-Beuve wrote about it, and the Académie française gave it a prize. A second collection, Poèmes et poésies, followed in 1855 and won another prize. In 1857 the General Council of Réunion, the assembly of his home island, voted him a yearly pension of about 2,000 francs. (A pension is money that a person receives regularly.) He also earned money by writing a Paris letter for the newspapers of the island. On 10 September 1857, in the church of Saint-Sulpice in Paris, Leconte de Lisle married Anne Adélaïde Perray, who was fifteen years younger than he was. The couple had no children. Family duties grew. His father had died in 1856 without leaving a fortune. At the end of 1859 his mother, and later two sisters, came to live in Paris near him. To feed everyone he began a long series of translations of the Greek poets (see below). His own poems appeared regularly in reviews, and in 1862 he collected them in his second great book, Poésies barbares (later Poèmes barbares). In 1865 Sainte-Beuve named him as one of the four living masters that young poets imitated, with Hugo, Gautier, and Banville. Fame came, but not money. The island had stopped his pension. Partly for this reason, in July 1864, he secretly accepted a pension of 300 francs a month from the private purse of the emperor, Napoléon III, to support his household and part of his family. For an old republican of 1848, this was a dangerous secret. Around 1860 a new generation of poets grew up in Paris. They shared a respect for careful work and beautiful form. The movement had several centers: Théophile Gautier and Théodore de Banville were also masters for the young poets, and the publisher Alphonse Lemerre and several small magazines held the group together. But the author of the Poèmes barbares became the most respected master of the group. Every Saturday evening he received the young poets in his small flat. Among them were Catulle Mendès, Sully Prudhomme, François Coppée, Léon Dierx, Paul Verlaine, Stéphane Mallarmé, and José-Maria de Heredia, one of his closest students. In 1866 Lemerre published a collection of new verse in small weekly parts, Le Parnasse contemporain. Parnassus is the mountain of the Muses in Greek mythology; from this title the group got its name. Two more series followed, in 1869–1871 and in 1876. In his official report of 1867, Gautier wrote that Leconte de Lisle had "all the qualities of a head of school". The man behind the legend was proud and shy at the same time. Witnesses describe his proud, upright appearance, his high bald forehead, and the monocle (a single eyeglass) that made him look colder than he was. His witty and cruel sayings about bad books traveled around Paris. The writer Edmond de Goncourt, after a dinner, noted that there was something of the actor and of the priest in his learned voice. In July 1870 France went to war against Prussia and lost terribly (see Franco-Prussian War). The empire fell, and the Republic was proclaimed. Leconte de Lisle stayed in Paris during the whole siege of the city, serving in the National Guard. His letters describe hunger, cold, and falling bombs. During these months came the worst public moment of his life. The new government published the private papers of the fallen emperor, and the secret pension appeared on the lists. The republican press attacked him. He answered in the newspaper Le Gaulois that he had never sold his pen to anyone and that hard necessity had forced him to accept the money. In the spring of 1871 came the Paris Commune, the revolt of the city of Paris, and its bloody end. He strongly opposed the Commune and was horrified by the violence of 1871. In a letter of 29 May 1871 he wrote that he was crying with despair. In 1870 and 1871 he also wrote three short political books: a Catéchisme populaire républicain (Popular Republican Catechism), a popular history of the French Revolution, and a popular history of Christianity. In simple questions and answers, they taught the ideas of a secular republic, that is, a state independent of any church: reason, justice, and the rule of the people. In January 1872 a conservative member of the National Assembly asked the government to take the author to court. The minister answered with a few empty sentences, and nothing happened. At the end of December 1871, the minister Jules Simon gave him a post at the library of the Luxembourg Palace in Paris. He succeeded the poet François Coppée. The records of the Senate date the decision to appoint him to 28 December 1871. According to Flottes, he formally took up the post of assistant librarian on 1 January 1873, with a yearly pay of 2,700 francs. His pay rose step by step to 4,200 francs. For the first time in his life, at over fifty, he had a safe income. The work was light. He sat every afternoon under the famous painted dome of Eugène Delacroix. His colleagues included the young Anatole France and his fellow islander, the poet Auguste Lacaussade. In 1872 he moved to 64 Boulevard Saint-Michel. He lived there for the last twenty-two years of his life, and his Saturday evenings continued there. The Académie française is a society of forty writers and thinkers. Leconte de Lisle presented himself in 1873 and in 1877, and failed both times. After the failure of 1877, Victor Hugo, who had voted for him, wrote to him that the Académie was useless to men like him, and that such men were necessary to it. Hugo died in 1885. At the national funeral, on 1 June 1885, Leconte de Lisle spoke in the name of the poets of France. He saluted, in the dead master, the sovereign poet whose songs had defended the weak and the oppressed. The next year, on 11 February 1886, he was elected to Hugo's seat. The official reception took place on 31 March 1887. His speech in praise of Hugo was openly republican and anticlerical (against the power of the Church in public life). The answer came from the playwright Alexandre Dumas the younger, son of the author of The Three Musketeers (see Alexandre Dumas). The ceremony honored the new member, but Dumas's speech also attacked his work. He said that Leconte de Lisle had emptied poetry of love and taught the praise of death, and he read the poem Midi aloud as an example. The old poet listened without moving. Official honors still came. The empire had given him the cross of the Legion of Honour in 1870, and the Republic made him an officer of the order in 1884. His health declined from about 1889. Around him, poetry was changing: a new school, the symbolists, wanted music, mystery, and free verse (see Symbolism). He attacked them with hard jokes, and old friendships suffered. But even the young rebels respected him. When they asked him in 1892 to preside at one of their banquets, he sent Mallarmé in his place with kind words. From 1888 he exchanged letters with Carmen Sylva, the queen of Romania, who wrote poems herself. Some of his last poems have a gentler tone. He returned to a Greece of light and love, and the island of his childhood appears again in them. Two months before his death he published a joyful Greek tale, L'Enlèvement d'Europèia. In the summer of 1894, while resting at a friend's house at Louveciennes, west of Paris, he caught pneumonia, a serious illness of the lungs. He died on 17 July 1894, at the age of seventy-five. The funeral service took place at Saint-Sulpice, and he was buried in the Montparnasse cemetery in Paris. At the grave, Heredia spoke for the poets and ended with the words: such was this impassive man. In two poems he had said his wish to sleep one day in the earth of his island. In September 1977 his remains were moved to Réunion and buried in the marine cemetery of Saint-Paul, beside the Indian Ocean. An empty monument, called a cenotaph, still marks his old grave in Paris. Leconte de Lisle published little and slowly. He corrected his poems for years before printing them. In 1891 he told the journalist Jules Huret that he had kept his first collection seven years in a drawer, and that he had burned four thousand verses. The Poèmes antiques (Ancient Poems) appeared at the end of November 1852: thirty-one poems and a preface that became a manifesto, that is, a public declaration of ideas (see below, "Ideas"). Most of the poems are Greek: stories of the myths, such as Niobé and Khirôn, and small bright pictures of ancient life in the manner of the Greek poet Theocritus. One group of poems turns to ancient India. In Bhagavat and La Vision de Brahma, Leconte de Lisle was one of the first French poets to bring themes of Hinduism into French verse. The book also contains Hypatie, on the Greek woman philosopher killed by a Christian crowd. The most famous poem placed in it today, Midi (Noon), was first collected in the Poèmes et poésies of 1855: Midi, roi des étés, épandu sur la plaine, Tombe en nappes d'argent des hauteurs du ciel bleu. (Literal English translation: "Noon, king of summers, spread over the plain, falls in sheets of silver from the heights of the blue sky.") The second great book appeared in 1862 as Poésies barbares and took its final name, Poèmes barbares (Barbarian Poems), in 1872. For Leconte de Lisle, "barbarian" meant everything outside the classical world of Greece: the Bible, the Middle Ages, the North of the Vikings, Egypt, Polynesia, and the tropical world of his island. The book opens with Qaïn (Cain), one of his best-known poems. Qaïn, the first murderer of the Bible, rises and answers the God who cursed him. He accuses this jealous God of having made evil itself, and announces that the oppressed human race will rise again. Pierre Flottes has shown the family tree of the poem. The English poet Byron had already defended Cain, and Lamartine had already accused the injustice of heaven. Leconte de Lisle carried their protest one step further. The poems are set in many parts of the world. Several of his best-known animal poems are in this book. In Les Éléphants, a caravan of elephants crosses the red desert. In Le Sommeil du condor, the great bird of the Andes sleeps standing in the icy night. There are poems of the North, taken from the old legends of Scandinavia (see Norse mythology). In one of them, Le Cœur de Hialmar, a dying Viking gives his heart to a raven to carry to the girl he loves. There are dark poems of the Middle Ages. The collection also includes several well-known poems about Réunion, such as Le Manchy. The book closes with Solvet seclum: one day the old, guilty earth will explode in space, and its dust will help to make new worlds. The Poèmes tragiques (Tragic Poems) came out in 1884. Many poems attack the crusades and the Inquisition with new violence. The book also contains poems of memory and love written in old age, such as L'Illusion suprême and Les Roses d'Ispahan, and the sea poems L'Albatros and Sacra fames, which use memories of his ocean voyages. The philosophical close of the book is La Maya: in this poem, all life and all history are Maya, the world seen as an illusion. After his death, his friends Heredia and the viscount de Guerne collected his remaining verse in the Derniers poèmes (Last Poems, 1895), together with his unfinished tragedy Frédégonde and his main critical articles. On 6 January 1873 the Odéon theater in Paris played Les Érinnyes (The Furies), his tragedy taken from Aeschylus, with stage music by the young Jules Massenet. One piece of this music, the "Élégie", later became one of Massenet's best-known short pieces. A second play, L'Apollonide (1888), was written to be set to music. The Belgian composer Franz Servais turned it into an opera, played in 1899, after the poet's death. For more than twenty years, Leconte de Lisle earned part of his living by translating the classics of Greece and Rome into French prose: Theocritus (1861), the Iliad (1867), the Odyssey (1868), Hesiod (1869), Aeschylus (1872), the Latin poet Horace (1873), Sophocles (1877), and Euripides (1884). He refused the elegant, free manner of older French translators. His translations used unfamiliar names, such as "Akhilleus" for "Achille", and a very literal, word-for-word style, in order to make Greek poetry seem less French. They influenced many readers and poets, although scholars criticized their mistakes and their heavy style; Edgard Pich notes that word-for-word exactness is not the same thing as faithfulness. Besides the three political books of 1870–1871, Leconte de Lisle left critical prose: the fighting prefaces of 1852, 1855, and 1861, a series of sharp articles on the living French poets (1864), and his speeches. Edgard Pich published a scholarly collection of these articles, prefaces, and speeches in 1971. They show that the "impassive" poet was also a fierce fighter with ideas. The central idea of Leconte de Lisle is impersonal poetry: poetry in which the writer does not talk about himself. In his time, the poets of Romanticism sang about their own loves and their own tears. Leconte de Lisle thought this was wrong twice over. First, he found it immodest. In the preface of 1852 he wrote that there is a useless vanity, and a lack of respect for sacred feelings, in telling the public the pains and pleasures of one's own heart. Second, he found it small: a poet who only talks about himself teaches nothing. His answer was the sonnet Les Montreurs (The Showmen, 1862), in which he compares the poet who sells his feelings to a chained animal shown to the crowd for money: Tel qu'un morne animal, meurtri, plein de poussière, La chaîne au cou, hurlant au chaud soleil d'été, Sur ton pavé cynique, ô plèbe carnassière ! (Literal English translation: "Like a sad animal, bruised, covered with dust, a chain on its neck, howling in the hot summer sun, whoever wishes may parade his bleeding heart on your cynical pavement, O flesh-eating crowd!") Impersonal does not mean without feeling. The poet puts his feelings into other beings: into Qaïn, into a condor, into a dying Viking. Irving Brown wrote in 1924 that his verse is like a Greek statue only in its solid form: the content remains full of emotion and life. The second great idea of the 1852 preface joins poetry and knowledge. Leconte de Lisle lived in the century of history and of the new science of religions, and he believed that the poet must be a scholar. He wrote in the preface: "And now science and art are turning back toward the common origins." The task of poetry, for him, was to bring the beliefs and the arts of the early ages of humanity back to life. For this, the poet needed exact knowledge. Before writing about India or about the Vikings, he studied the translations and the collections of the scholars of his time. Caroline De Mulder has shown that science was also a weapon for him: the science that explains the origins of life stood, in his mind, against the teachings of the Church. Leconte de Lisle did not believe in God, but few poets have written so much about gods. For him, every religion was true in its own hour, because every religion was the ideal form of the dreams and hopes of a people. The gods are born, grow old, and die with the peoples who dreamed them. One of his late poems is called Le Dernier Dieu (The Last God, 1885). Two ancient worlds held a special place in his work. Greece was for him the world of beauty and light, where human beings were free and respected. India taught the opposite lesson: that the visible world is an illusion, and that the tired soul wants rest. Here he used nineteenth-century European ideas about Hinduism and Buddhism, which were often not exact. In his poems, Maya represents the world as an illusion, and Nirvana becomes an image of release from suffering. His view of the Christian churches was much more hostile. He respected the person of Jesus, and his poem Le Nazaréen pities the crucified man whose message was betrayed. But he hated the Church as a power. In his poems, he often describes the Middle Ages as a time of terror, religious violence, and torture. Caroline De Mulder has shown that this dark Middle Age is a political picture. Leconte de Lisle turns the beloved Middle Ages of the romantic writers upside down. He uses the tools of the "gothic" horror story against the Church of his own century, and De Mulder calls his medieval poems a "republican gothic". Leconte de Lisle is often called a pessimist, that is, a person who believes that life is bad and hope is useless. His poems say terrible things: life is a dark accident, history is a river of blood, the earth itself will die. But Irving Brown explained that a pessimist of this kind is a disappointed optimist: his pessimism grew partly from his disappointed political hopes after 1848. And the darkness is never complete. The same man loved the sun, the sea, animals, energy, and glory, and his poems about death are written in verses full of light and force. For a long time, critics said that Leconte de Lisle left politics completely after 1848. The book of Caroline De Mulder, Leconte de Lisle, entre utopie et république (2005), has shown that this picture is false. Before 1848 his politics was a utopia, the perfect society of Fourier. After 1848 it became simpler: a secular republic without a king, independent of the Church. He rarely wrote poems directly about the political events of his own time; À l'Italie and Le Sacre de Paris, born from the wars of 1859 and 1870, are exceptions. He usually expressed his republican ideas through poems set in the past. His Greece, where law rules and human beings are respected, is a picture of the good society. His Middle Ages is a picture of the enemy. His rebels and heretics, from Qaïn to the prophet of Le Talion, speak for the oppressed of all ages. In this sense, De Mulder concludes, his political beliefs helped to shape his whole work. The alexandrine, the classical French line of twelve syllables, was his main form. He also used other regular meters and several stanza forms, such as quatrains (stanzas of four lines) and sonnets. He valued strict meter, clear grammar, and carefully placed rhymes. Pierre Flottes notes that the importance of rhyme in his verse should not be confused with a search for "rich" rhyme: his rhymes are often the ones the ear expects, because he did not try to surprise. His students said that they learned from his slow, deep reading what a well-made verse is. Description has an important place in his poetry. In Brown's comparison of six French poets, Leconte de Lisle used about twice as many sensory images as any of the others, and images of movement were especially frequent in his verse. His animal poems treated animals in a new way in French poetry. In them the animal is not a symbol of man, as in the old fables, but a living being with its own movements, instincts, and place in nature. Unlike many of the places in his historical poems, Réunion came from his own memories. He left his island at twenty-six and never returned. But his memories of it shaped his use of light and color. They gave him the sea, the tropical night, and the burning noon of his most loved poems, such as Le Manchy, La Ravine Saint-Gilles, and La Fontaine aux lianes. A last detail of his style amused his contemporaries: he wrote Greek and other foreign names in a new way, closer to their original sound ("Klytaimnestra", "Kirkè", "Qaïn"), as a mark of respect for other worlds. Victor Hugo was the writer who influenced him most. Les Orientales had made him a poet. His Poèmes barbares treat the same great historical matter as Hugo's La Légende des siècles. And he ended in Hugo's seat at the Académie. With Charles Baudelaire he exchanged respect: each wrote a serious article about the other. In 1892 Leconte de Lisle presided over the committee for a monument to Baudelaire. His students continued his work in different ways. Heredia condensed the master's vast historical visions into the hundred sonnets of Les Trophées (1893). Even the founders of Symbolism passed through his school: the first book of Paul Verlaine, Poèmes saturniens (1866), praises the poets "who chisel words like cups / and make deeply moved verses very coldly". The Symbolists first learned from the Parnassians and later rejected many of their rules. Judgments about Leconte de Lisle were strong on both sides. Sainte-Beuve named him in 1865 as one of the four living masters of French poetry. Victor Hugo wrote to him in 1877 that men like him were necessary to the Académie. On the other side, Alexandre Dumas the younger, in 1887, accused him of emptying poetry of love and of teaching the praise of death. The scholars who studied him later were also divided. Edmond Estève judged that the work has faults of coldness and length, but that its best parts are among the most solid monuments of French poetry. Irving Brown wrote that, if perfection of form is the measure, France has produced no more perfect poet. At the poet's funeral, Heredia summed up the work: a powerful magician who had called up the gods, the vanished civilizations, the wild beasts and the faraway lands. When Leconte de Lisle died in 1894, Symbolism had become the leading movement among younger poets. In the twentieth century his fame declined. Readers found his poetry too long, too learned, and too cold, and schoolbooks kept only a few pieces, such as Midi, Les Éléphants, and Le Cœur de Hialmar. Outside France he was never widely known, though the English poet Swinburne admired him. Edmond Estève noted one interesting case: the young Indian poet Toru Dutt, writing in English in Calcutta, translated him and learned from him. Scholars continued to study his work during the twentieth century. In July 1898 a monument by the sculptor Denys Puech was placed in the Luxembourg garden, near his library. It was paid for with money collected from the public. In 1934 a plaque was placed on his last home, 64 Boulevard Saint-Michel. Edmond Estève wrote the classic French study of the man and the work (1922), and Irving Brown presented him to American readers (1924). Pierre Flottes retold his life (1954). Edgard Pich published a scholarly collection of his articles, prefaces, and speeches (1971) and later prepared a complete critical edition of the poems. Caroline De Mulder (2005) showed the political meaning that runs through the whole work. His work also helped prepare the way for some of the Symbolist poets. On his island he was never forgotten. Réunion sees him as one of the fathers of its literature, and streets, squares, and schools there carry his name. In September 1977 his remains were moved from Paris to the marine cemetery of Saint-Paul, near the places of his childhood. Poèmes antiques (1852; enlarged editions later). Poèmes et poésies (1855; later divided between the two main books). Poèmes barbares (first edition 1862, under the title Poésies barbares; final form 1872). Poèmes tragiques (1884). Derniers poèmes (1895, published after his death). Les Érinnyes, tragedy after Aeschylus (played 1873). L'Apollonide, a play written to be set to music (1888). Translations into French prose: Theocritus (1861), the Iliad (1867), the Odyssey (1868), Hesiod (1869), Aeschylus (1872), Horace (1873), Sophocles (1877), Euripides (1884). Political prose: Catéchisme populaire républicain (1870) and two popular histories (1871).

Lee Byung-chull (Korean:이병철;李秉喆, February 12, 1910 – November 19, 1987) was a South Korean businessman and trader. He was a founder of Samsung Electronics, Samsung Heavy Industries and many Samsung group companies.

Lee Ae-ran (Hangul = 이애란; Revised Romanization = I Aeran; McCune–Reischauer = Ri Aeran) (born 1964) is a South Korean activist. In 2010 she received the International Women of Courage Award. Lee's grandparents left North Korea to go to South Korea. The government of North Korea sent Lee and her family to a labor camp. She was in jail for eight years. In 1997, a family member in America wrote a book. The book said Lee's father worked against North Korea, so Lee ran away to South Korea. Lee studied the subject of food and nutrition at Ewha Womans University. In 2009, she received a PhD. In 2005, Lee started the Global Leadership Scholarship Program. The program gives scholarships to students from North Korea to learn English. In 2008, Lee ran for a seat in the National Assembly. She was the first North Korean defector to do this. In 2009, Lee started the Hana Defector Women's Organization. The NGO helps North Korean women who live in South Korea. The women receive job training, childcare, help with education, and human rights training. Lee became the head of the North Korean Traditional Food Institute in 2012. The institute tries to bring North and South Korea closer together. It gives vocational training to North Korean defectors. It also teaches about the food traditions of Pyongyang. Also in 2012, Lee led an 18-day hunger strike in front of the Chinese embassy. Lee protested against China, because they wanted to send North Korean refugees back to North Korea. Lee received a 2010 International Women of Courage Award from the U.S. Department of State.

Lee Chambers (born 22 May 1985) is a British psychologist, entrepreneur and radio host. He is the founder of both PhenomGames and Essentialise Workplace Wellbeing. Chambers has been interviewed by Vogue (magazine), The Guardian, and Newsweek and he is known for analyzing the psychological aspects of color and workplaces. Chambers holds a BSc in International Business Psychology and an MSc in Environmental Psychology from the University of Surrey. Chambers founded the video game company PhenomGames in 2008. He has worked as a performance psychologist for sports clubs, including Manchester City F.C and Everton F.C. In 2020, he sold PhenomGames to Dangaard. Lee Chambers is the founder of Essentialise Workplace Wellbeing, a company that delivers mental wellbeing initiatives to other organizations. He is also a Director of Wellbeing Lancashire, a Community Interest Company specializing in health innovation and equality, and has worked with a variety of notable companies, including Indeed, TalkTalk, and Anytime Fitness. Chambers is the host of the Self Aware Entrepreneur Show and was voted in the Top 50 BAME Entrepreneurs Under 50 in 2020 alongside Nitin Passi, Eric Yuan and Rangan Chatterjee. Chambers has recorded over 100 podcasts that includes episodes with Jamal Edwards, Josh Elledge and Leah Totton. He has also been recognized for his entrepreneurial journey by Startups.co.uk with Anne Boden, Ben Francis and Steven Bartlett. In 2020, Chambers was nominated for the Lancashire Business View awards. Top 50 BAME Entrepreneur Under 50 of 2020. UK Enterprise Awards Organisational Psychologist of the Year 2021.

Lee Hyeon-seo (, born January 1980) is a North Korean defector and activist. She is known for her book, The Girl with Seven Names. Lee lives in Seoul, South Korea. She is a student. She escaped North Korea and later helped her family escape through China and Laos. Lee Hyeon-seo grew up in Hyesan, North Korea, believing her country was the best and feeling proud, even though she saw a public execution at age seven. Despite her family's relative comfort, the North Korean famine caused widespread suffering and death. In 1997, Lee crossed the frozen Yalu River with the help of a friendly border guard. She only meant to stay for a little while and then go back. But things got complicated, and she had to live with her relatives in China as an illegal immigrant. Lee bought the identity of a mentally challenged girl from Heilongjiang. With it, she got a passport and driver's license. At one point, after being accused of being North Korean, she was interrogated by police and tested on her Chinese language skills and what she knew about China. Thanks to her father's insistence that she learn Chinese when she was younger, she was able to pass the test. After 10 years of being a fugitive in China, Lee managed to escape to South Korea.Upon arriving at Incheon International Airport in January 2008, she identified herself as an asylum-seeker. Officials quickly took her to another room to check her papers and verify her identity. They warned her that if she broke Korean law, she would be detained and then deported back to China. Lee requested that they contact the National Intelligence Service, which then transported her to downtown Seoul three hours later. She went through an orientation for life in South Korea and was given a house to live in. At first, she felt both scared and excited, but settling in was harder than she expected. She noticed significant differences between North and South Korea in education, culture, and language, despite their shared ethnicity. She endured anti-North Korean prejudice and sometimes thought "It would be so much easier to return to China." However, after a year of confusion, she eventually found meaning in her new life. Lee learned that North Korean police had intercepted money she sent to her family and that her mother and brother were about to be sent to a remote area. Worried and knowing they couldn't speak Chinese, she decided to go back for them. She returned to China, met her family in Changbai, and her brother helped their mother cross the border. She guided them on a 2000-mile journey through China, where they nearly got caught several times. When stopped and questioned by a police officer, Lee claimed her family was deaf and mute and didn't speak Chinese. The officer believed her and let them go. At the Lao border, Lee paid a broker to help her mother and brother get to the South Korean Embassy in Vientiane. However, while she was traveling to China to return to South Korea, she learned that her mother and brother had been caught crossing the border. She then traveled to Luang Namtha, Laos, where she paid a bribe and fine. After a month of ordeals her family members were released. She traveled with them to Vientiane, but her family was arrested and jailed near the South Korean embassy. Lee went back and forth between the immigration office and the National Police Agency for almost 50 days, "desperately trying to get my family out … but I didn't have enough money to pay the bribes. I lost all hope." An English-speaking Australian named Dick Stolp helped her by paying the remaining amount needed for her family and two other North Koreans to get out of jail. When she asked why he was helping, he said it was for the North Korean people, not just her. She saw this as a significant moment that represented hope and the support of strangers and the international community for North Koreans. She later said that this encounter marked the moment "when my view of the world changed and I realized there were many good people on this planet. I also realized how precious life is." Soon she and her family were living in South Korea. In 2011, Lee wrote that she was learning English "to boost [her] prospects," noting that North Koreans' "lack of English is a handicap" on the job market. In China, she spent a lot of time learning Chinese but didn't expect to face so much stress about the language in South Korea. She worked part-time, took accounting classes, and earned the necessary certifications. In 2011, she was specially admitted to the Chinese language department at Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, hoping to be involved in growing trade with China. She noted that she was working as a student journalist at South Korea's Ministry of Unification with South Korean college students, writing about North-South Korea relations and reunification. Additionally, she was one of 50 North Korean escapees in the 'English for the Future' program sponsored by the British Embassy in Seoul, which helps her maintain her English studies. She was doing volunteer work "out of gratitude for all the aid [she has] received since [she] came here and of hope to return the favor to other people in need." As of May 2014, Lee was still studying at the Hankuk University of Foreign Studies and working as a student journalist with the Ministry of Unification. Lee shared her experiences at a TED conference in Long Beach, California. Her talk has over 18 million views on YouTube. In May 2013, she reunited with Australian Dick Stolp on an Australian TV program, where she praised him as a modern hero. Stolp felt proud to see her doing good work and felt he had helped her change her life. She has been interviewed by the BBC, CNN, CBS News, and many other TV and radio outlets around the world. Lee has also been interviewed by major media outlets worldwide, spoke at the Oslo Freedom Forum in May 2014, and executive produced the PBS documentary Beyond Utopia about South Korean pastor Kim Sungeun, which aired on January 9, 2024.

Lee Albert Miglin (July 12, 1924 – May 4, 1997) was an American real estate developer, businessman, and philanthropist. He was born in Westville, Illinois. Miglin went on to become a successful real estate developer in partnership with J. Paul Beitler. Miglin was born in Westville, Illinois. He trained as an air cadet during World War II, before attending the University of Illinois. In 1988, Miglin-Beitler Developments revealed plans to build a 1,999 foot 125-floor skyscraper in Chicago to be called the Miglin-Beitler Skyneedle. This would have been the tallest building in the world at the time of its planned completion. However, the building was never built. Miglin-Beitler had held hopes of creating the project, but these plans would never happen following Miglin's murder. Miglin was murdered at his garage in Chicago's Gold Coast neighborhood on May 4, 1997 by serial killer Andrew Cunanan. He was 72 years old. He had been tortured with a saw and a screwdriver, his ribs had been broken, he had been beaten and stabbed, and his throat had been slashed with a gardener's bow saw. The second season of the anthology television series American Crime Story: The Assassination of Gianni Versace, was about the Cunanan spree where Miglin was played by Mike Farrell. In 1959, Miglin married 20-year-old Marilyn Klecka. She was a businesswoman and host of several shows on the Home Shopping Network. They had two children together, Marlena (born 1968) and Duke Miglin (born 1971).

Lee Stephen Mason (born 29 October 1971) is the English professional referee who was video assistant referee primarily in the Premier League. He was born in Sunderland. He was sacked as video assistant referee after incorrectly allowed Ivan Toney's goal in the Premier League match on 11th February 2023 and it was Arsenal versus Brentford. Mason is a former chairman of Sunderland’s Referees' Society and is associated with the North East County Football Association. He attended Thornleigh College in Bolton and then the Liverpool Institute of Higher Education between 1990 and 1993, living in Newman Hall, where he gained his degree. Whilst there he played for his college football team as well as being a regular compere, hosting a variety of social events at a students' union club. Mason's younger brother, Andy, is a former professional footballer who was a trainee at Bolton Wanderers, and played professionally for Hull City, among others, before ending up playing in Non-League. He retired from on-field duties at the end of the 2020–21 season, but will become the league's first dedicated Video Assistant Referee from the 2021—22 season.

Lenore "Lee" Krasner (born Lena Krassner; October 27, 1908 – June 19, 1984) was an American abstract expressionist painter. She also worked in other media such as mosaics and especially collage. Krasner was influenced by George Bridgman and Hans Hoffman. Krasner was important within abstraction. She connected early-20th-century art with the new ideas of postwar America. She is also one of the few female artists to have a retrospective show at the Museum of Modern Art. She also had a retrospective exhibit at the Barbican Arts Center, London.

Caroline Lee Radziwiłł (née Bouvier; March 3, 1933 – February 15, 2019) was an American socialite. She was the younger sister of former US First Lady Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis. Radziwill was born Caroline Lee Bouvier at Doctors Hospital in New York, New She was the second daughter of wealthy stockbroker John Vernou Bouvier III and Janet Norton Lee. Her older sister was Jacqueline Lee Bouvier (1929-1994), future First Lady of the United States. She also had a step-sister and a step-brother, Janet (1945-1985) and James Auchincloss (b. 1947). They were the children of her mother by her second husband Hugh D. Auchincloss. She has been known as "Lee" since childhood. Like her older sister, she was educated at selective schools for high society girls. She graduated from Miss Porter's in 1951. Radziwill married three times. Her first husband was Michael Canfield, a publishing executive. They married on April 18, 1953, and moved to London, England. They divorced in 1958. She married Prince Stanislas Radziwill on March 19, 1959. They had two children; Anthony (1959-1999) and Christina (b. 1960). They divorced in 1974. She then moved back to the United States, where she married film director Herbert Ross, on September 23, 1988. They divorced in 2001 shortly before Ross's death. In March 1962, Radziwill went with her sister Jacqueline Kennedy, then First Lady, on a goodwill tour of India and Pakistan. In the 1960s, Radziwill tried a career as an actress. She was unsuccessful. She later tried interior decoration with some success. Her son Anthony died of cancer in August 1999, one month after the death in a plane crash of her nephew John F. Kennedy Jr.. She lived in Paris, France. Radziwill died on February 15, 2019 in New York City, aged 85.

Leland "Lee" Remmel (June 30, 1924 – April 16, 2015) was an American football personality. He was known for working 62 years with the Green Bay Packers as a sportswriter and later a team employee (public relations, historian, spokesperson, and writer). Remmel was born in Shawano, Wisconsin. He was married to Margaret "Noreen" Remmel from 1948 until her death on April 27, 2012. Remmel died on April 16, 2015 in Green Bay, Wisconsin, aged 90.

Sir David Lee Pearson (born 4 February 1974) is a Paralimpic champion on horse riding. He won fourteen gold medals. He is called the "Godfather" of para-dressage. Lee Pearson was born on 4 February 1974 in, England, with a medical condition called. In 1980, when he was 6, Margaret Thatcher carried (lifted) him up the stairs in 10 Downing Street. Thatcher also gave him the "Children of Courage" award. He wanted to go to the Paralympic Games since he watched the 1996 Summer Paralympics. Pearson won three gold medals at the 2000 Summer Paralympics in Sydney, three golds at the 2004 Summer Paralympics in Athens, and three more golds at the 2008 Summer Paralympics in Beijing. He and his horse Gentleman won a gold, a silver and a bronze medal at the 2012 Summer Paralympics in London. He and his horse Zion won a gold and a silver at the 2016 Summer Paralympics in Rio de Janeiro. He and his horse Breezer won three gold medals at the 2020 Summer Paralympics in Tokyo. Pearson raised Breezer since he was a foal (baby horse). Pearson is gay. He was the first British Paralympic champion to come out, when he was 20. He is also a LGBTQ+ rights activist.

Loreley "Lee" June Phillip Bell (June 10, 1928 – February 25, 2020) was an American talk show host and soap opera creator. During her career on Chicago television, she hosted over 10,000 programs. Her best known works were The Bold and the Beautiful and The Young and the Restless. Bell was born in Chicago. Bell died on February 25, 2020 at her home in Beverly Hills, California at the age of 91.

Lee Toong Leon, better known as Leon Lee, is a Malaysian businessman, public speaker and entrepreneur based in Penang, Malaysia. He is the founder and current CEO of Zeon Properties Group, a Malaysian property consultancy firm with more than 500 personnel and agents in Malaysia, China, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Singapore, Vietnam and Indonesia. Leon has been awarded the Distinguished Conduct Medal (Pingat Kelakuan Terpuji) in 2016 and the Meritorious Service Medal (Pingat Jasa Kebaktian) in 2010 by Penang State Governor, Tun Abdul Rahman Abbas for his services to the state. A King Scout since 2000, Leon also received the National King Scout's Merit Award in 2010. Leon was born in George Town, Penang, Malaysia on 29 March 1982. He attended Penang Chinese Girls Primary School and Chung Hwa Confucian High School. Leon obtained his bachelor's degree in Computer Science from University of Northumbria at Newcastle. After graduating with his degree, Leon founded Zeon Computer (M) Sdn Bhd, a chain of IT stores providing IT supplies and solutions. The business spread to 5 branches all over Malaysia, employing more than 30 people and was eventually bought over by a public listed company. He founded Zeon Properties in Penang in November 2012 and is the current CEO. It is positioned as a real estate agency that helps clients invest, sell, or lease residential and commercial properties in the market. Besides real estate and marketing, the company also specialises in real estate investment advisory, foreign direct investment, international project marketing, retail and planning consultancy. It sources for the best property and infrastructure opportunities, and works with investment partners to fund investment opportunities. It is also involved in the Malaysia My Second Home programme, property development and management, offering the best of services with the highest professionalism and efficiency to help enhance the property value over time. Just a year after the founding of Zeon Properties, Leon successfully negotiated with the publisher of the largest English daily in Malaysia - Star Media Group Berhad - and became the event partner of the corporation's long-running property fair, StarProperty.my Fair. After teaming up with Star Media Group for four years, Leon moved on to work with Guang Ming Daily, one of the largest northern region Chinese newspaper in Malaysia, to hold the Guang Ming Property Fair in 2017. Ten property developers rode the week-long fair to promote their projects, while Zeon Properties provided a myriad of entertainment to keep the attention of the crowd, including a cheongsam fashion show and live entertainment performances. Wanting to offer a plethora of properties for buyers to choose from, Leon negotiated with property developers and as of 2017, became the marketing partner of more than 90 property projects. He was one of the earliest property marketing consultants in Penang to predict and measure the impact of vital infrastructure and transport links to the state's property sector, pointing to a doubling of property prices near the second Penang bridge in 2014: "In 2007, a terrace house in Batu Maung was worth about RM700,000. But now, a similar unit is priced at RM1.4mil". Leon has been a keynote speaker at various international events including SP Setia's event in Singapore, The Star Property Fair and Guang Ming Property Fair. He has been featured in multiple international publications including Wall Street Select, Daily Herald and Digital Journal. Leon is also the founder of Auto Mall in Penang. Intertwining his social life with business networking, Leon currently serves the Consul-General of the People's Republic of China in Penang as its consular protection liaison officer. He is also the All-China Federation of Returned Overseas Chinese Youth Committee member. He has also been appointed as the Committee Member and Youth Committee Deputy Chief of Sichuan Overseas Exchange Association of the People's Republic of China. He is a National Council Member of the Associated Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry Malaysia (ACCCIM) Penang Chinese Chamber of Commerce, National Chairman of the ACCCIM Young Entrepreneurs Committee, chairman of the Penang Chinese Chamber of Commerce (PCCC) Young Entrepreneurs Section, PCCC General committee member and was head of property management of the Property Development, Construction and Management Committee. He is the Deputy chairman of ASEAN Retail-Chains & Franchise Federation and Vice President of Penang's Fort Cornwallis 1786. In 2018, he completed a Ministerial Workshop on "Forging Closer Partnership to implement 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda for Developing Countries", which was sponsored by the Ministry of Commerce, People's Republic of China. The same year also saw him being elected as the chairman of the Penang Scouts Council for the 2018–2020 term. In 2017, he took part in the Youth Entrepreneurs Economy Workshop organised by the Overseas Chinese Affairs Office of the State Council at Beijing University. He was the founder and first organising chairman of the Top 50 Enterprise Awards 2007 of the Young Entrepreneurs Association of Malaysia. He went on to become the association's Penang chairman. He was also the president of Junior Chamber International United Penang in 2008. He is State Adviser of Malaysia Entrepreneurs Development Association and was its Penang chairman from 2010 to 2014. Of note is the Zeon Charity Club, where he and his team launch social work from contributing to religious institutions to hosting birthday lunches and annual feasts in an old folks home in Penang and also distributing meals to the homeless at the gates of the Goddess of Mercy Temple in Jalan Masjid Kapitan Kling, George Town.

Lee Yi-hsiu (; born on 10 June 1988), known as History Bro (Chinese: 歷史哥), is a Taiwanese political activist, radio personality, and Internet celebrity. Lee has a master's degree. Lee supported Han Kuo-yu. Born in 1988, and raised in Kaohsiung, he has a YouTube channel.

Leet (sometimes written as "1337" or "l33t"), also known as eleet or leet-speak, is another alphabet for the English language that is used mostly on the internet. It uses various combinations of ASCII characters to replace Latinate letters. For example, leet spellings of the word leet include 1337 and l33t; eleet may be spelled 31337 or 3l33t. It is used on the internet in forums, chat rooms and online games. Leet is mostly used for English, but can also be used with other languages including French, Spanish and German. Leet-speak is a mixture of words (mostly computer-related jargon) spelled incorrectly intentionally*, usually coming from typographical errors (e.g. the becomes t3h). The words of Leet-speak are usually put together to create a dialect (small language). This dialect is used in some places for funniness. l33tspeak uses numbers, ASCII symbols, and diacritics together to make symbols that look like Latin letters. For example, the name "David" would translate in 1337 as |)/-\\/1|) or more commonly as D4v1d. Most of the time it is only the vowels that are changed and then usually only they are replaced by numbers. Therefore, it is unusual to see someone use the leet alphabet to spell out a whole word (although there are common exceptions, namely 1337). These are only examples; these are not mandatory for Leet-speak, which is not officially defined anywhere, like most slangs.
