She loved the letters of Madame de Sévigné, a great writer of the 17th century, and she passed this love to her daughter and her grandsons. This grandmother later became the model for the narrator's grandmother, one of the most loved figures of the novel. Adrien and Jeanne married on 3 September 1870. Adolphe Crémieux was one of the witnesses. Jeanne promised that her children would be baptized, but she refused to change her own religion. So Marcel grew up between two worlds: a Catholic world from his father and a Jewish world from his mother. This mixed family background remained important in his life and in his book. Marcel was born in a terrible time for France. The country had just lost the Franco-Prussian War against Germany. Paris had been hungry and cold during a long siege. Then came the fighting of the Paris Commune in the spring of 1871. Because of the danger, Adrien Proust took his pregnant wife out of the city center. They went to Auteuil, a green area at the edge of Paris. There, in the house and garden that Jeanne's uncle Louis Weil had bought in 1857, at 96 rue La Fontaine, Marcel was born at eleven in the evening of 10 July 1871. The baby was very weak. For a while the family feared he would die. He lived, and on 5 August 1871 he was baptized in the church of Saint-Louis-d'Antin in Paris. His only brother, Robert, was born on 24 May 1873. Robert was strong and healthy. Later he became a famous surgeon, like their father. The family moved to a large flat at 9 boulevard Malesherbes in Paris. Marcel's childhood had two happy places outside the flat in Paris. Both were gardens, and both entered his novel. The first was Auteuil. Every spring and summer the family stayed in the big house and park of great-uncle Louis Weil, where Marcel was born. Three generations of the family met there, around the joking old uncle and the grandmother full of stories. In the garden grew chestnut trees, lilacs, and hawthorns, the flowering bushes that fill the most poetic pages of the novel. In the summer of 1881 the grandmother even took the young Marcel, alone with her, to the seaside town of Cabourg. The second was Illiers, his father's home town. From the time Marcel was six, the family went there at Easter. Marcel stayed in the house of his aunt and uncle, Élisabeth and Jules Amiot. He read for hours in the garden. He walked by the small river and in a park called the Pré Catelan. Later, in his novel, Proust mixed Illiers and Auteuil together. From them he made an imaginary town called Combray. It is the town of the narrator's childhood. In 1971, a hundred years after Proust's birth, the real town formally changed its name to Illiers-Combray, in honor of the book. When Marcel was nine years old, something happened that changed his life. In the spring of 1881 he was coming home from a family walk in the Bois de Boulogne. Suddenly he could not breathe. He was choking so badly that his parents thought he was dying. It was his first big attack of asthma. His father, a great doctor, could do little. Another doctor was called and gave the boy an injection of morphine, without any effect. That night, the story says, they had to sit the boy up straight in bed, held by piles of heavy medical books. From then on, Marcel was a fragile child. Flowers, dust, smoke, and country air could start an attack. The Easter stays in Illiers had to stop. His mother watched over him all the time. This deep love between the sick boy and his worried mother became a key part of his novel. The most famous scene of the novel draws on this childhood. The little narrator cannot sleep until his mother comes upstairs to kiss him goodnight. One evening she does not come, because there is a guest. The boy waits on the stairs, sick with sadness. This "goodnight kiss" scene opens the whole book. In the autumn of 1882, at eleven, Marcel entered a well-known school in Paris, then called the Lycée Fontanes. Soon afterwards it took back its old name, Condorcet. He often missed class because of his asthma. Still, he read a great deal and wrote very well. At school he found close friends: Jacques Bizet, son of the composer of Carmen, whom he had already met in primary school; Daniel Halévy; Robert Dreyfus; and others. With them he talked endlessly about books. Together they also made little class magazines, copied by hand, with names like Le Lundi and La Revue lilas. After class the boys played in the gardens of the Champs-Élysées. There Marcel fell in love, in a child's way, with a Russian girl named Marie de Benardaky. He never forgot her. She later gave some traits to Gilberte, the narrator's first love in the novel. In his last school year, Marcel had a philosophy teacher named Alphonse Darlu. Marcel admired him greatly. After only two days of class, he wrote Darlu a long, strange letter about his own divided mind. Darlu made him love philosophy for life. Years later, Proust went back to him for private lessons while studying for his degree. In November 1889, at eighteen, Proust joined the army as a one-year volunteer. On 11 November he signed up. Four days later he joined the 76th infantry regiment in the city of Orléans. Everyone expected the worst for this fragile, dreamy young man. In fact the year went well. He was allowed to sleep in a rented room in town, and his officers were kind to him. At a dinner given by the prefect of the region, in February 1890, he met another young volunteer serving in Orléans, Robert de Billy, who stayed a friend for life. During this army year he also suffered a serious loss: in January 1890 his beloved grandmother Adèle died of uremia, the same illness that would later kill his mother. His slow, delayed sorrow for her already looked like what the novel would one day call the "intermittences of the heart". Proust even kept a happy memory of the army. Years later, in a friend's question album, he was asked which military act he admired most. He answered: his own year of service. Question albums like this one were a fashion of the time. One of them later became famous as the "Proust Questionnaire". His captain, Count Walewski, came from the family of Napoleon. Proust watched him with delight. This officer later helped to inspire the captain de Borodino in the novel. Back in Paris in November 1890, Proust signed up to study law. He also joined the École libre des sciences politiques, a famous school of politics, where he found his friend Robert de Billy again. He was not a bad student. In 1892 he passed his oral exams in politics with good marks. Later he also got his degree in law. Then, at the end of 1893, he began a degree in philosophy, partly at the Sorbonne and partly through private lessons. He followed the courses of the philosophers Émile Boutroux and Paul Janet, and received his degree on 30 March 1895, ranked twenty-third among the 118 candidates. But he did not want any of the jobs his father hoped for. He tried two weeks in a lawyer's office and hated it. He said no to diplomacy, no to the courts, no to business. In 1895 he sat a small exam for an unpaid post at the Mazarine, a great library in Paris. He ranked third among the three successful candidates. There were three posts. He almost never went to work. He asked for leave again and again. On 1 March 1900 the administration finally counted him as having resigned. To his father this looked like a wasted life. In truth, the young man had already chosen his real work: watching people, and writing. In the Paris of that time, rich families opened their homes on fixed days. Guests came to talk, to hear music, and to meet famous people. Such a meeting, and the room it happened in, was called a salon. Proust loved the salons. From the age of seventeen he went from one to another. People laughed at him a little and called him a snob, a person who runs after grand names. But he was also studying this world, like a scientist studies insects. He was welcomed by Geneviève Straus, a woman of famous wit who had first been married to the composer Georges Bizet. He met the writer Anatole France in the salon of Madame Arman de Caillavet. At Madeleine Lemaire's, a painter of flowers, he heard the best musicians of Paris. In April 1893, at Madeleine Lemaire's, he met Count Robert de Montesquiou, a proud poet and dandy with a sharp tongue. Through him Proust reached the oldest French nobility, including the beautiful Countess Greffulhe. Montesquiou later gave many traits to the Baron de Charlus, one of the great characters of the novel. At the start of 1892 a group of young men, most of them old Condorcet friends, decided to start a small magazine: the poet Fernand Gregh, Daniel Halévy, Robert Dreyfus, Louis de La Salle and others. Jacques Bizet brought Proust to the first meeting. They called the review Le Banquet ("The Banquet"), after a book by the Greek philosopher Plato, and in honor of the teaching of their master Darlu. The first issue appeared in March 1892, printed in four hundred copies; Gregh soon became its editor. There were eight issues in all, until March 1893. Proust wrote short pieces for it: portraits, little stories, thoughts about love and fashion. When Le Banquet died, he wrote for a bigger magazine, La Revue blanche. There his texts appeared next to those of famous writers such as Mallarmé and André Gide. In those same weeks, Proust's path crossed the path of a man he would often be compared to. On 7 January 1892 his mother's cousin Louise Neuburger married the philosopher Henri Bergson, and Marcel was one of the attendants at the wedding. Bergson also wrote about time and memory, and many readers later looked for his ideas behind the novel. But the two cousins never became close, and in the long interview he gave when Swann's Way came out, Proust said plainly that his book was not a "Bergsonian novel". On 22 May 1894, at an evening in the Paris salon of Madeleine Lemaire, Proust met a young musician named Reynaldo Hahn. He was still a teenager, born in Caracas, in Venezuela, and already a brilliant composer and singer. Hahn sang his own songs for Marcel, above all his settings of poems by Verlaine, in a soft voice that all Paris praised. On 18 August of that year, Madeleine Lemaire invited them both for a month to Réveillon, her castle east of Paris. There the friendship of the two young men turned into love. Their romance lasted about two years. After it ended, they stayed the closest of friends for the rest of Proust's life. Some pains of this love entered the novel. One evening Hahn refused to ride home with Proust after a party. Proust turned this small wound into a famous scene: Odette going home in the Verdurins' carriage instead of Swann's. Hahn was one of the very few people allowed into Proust's room during his last illness in 1922. On 12 June 1896 Proust published his first book, Les Plaisirs et les Jours (Pleasures and Days). It collected his short stories, portraits, and poems. It was a luxury book, printed in only 1,500 copies. Anatole France wrote the preface. Madeleine Lemaire painted flowers for it. Reynaldo Hahn wrote four piano pieces for the poems. It cost 13 francs 50, at a time when a normal book cost 3 francs 50. The book sold very badly: in twenty-two years, only 329 copies left the publisher's stock. Critics saw only a gifted rich young man playing at literature. Even his friends teased him. In the winter of 1897, in a private show of shadow puppets, they played a sketch laughing at the price of the book, adding up the famous names inside it franc by franc. Today readers see the book differently. Its themes, time, memory, sadness, and forgetting, already point toward the great novel to come. On 3 February 1897 the writer Jean Lorrain attacked Pleasures and Days in a newspaper. Worse, he hinted in an ugly way at Proust's private life and his friendship with young Lucien Daudet. Proust answered in the way of the time: he challenged Lorrain to a duel. A duel was a formal fight, with strict rules, to defend one's honor. The two men met on 6 February 1897 in the woods of Meudon, near Paris, with pistols, at twenty-five paces. Proust's witnesses were the painter Jean Béraud and a famous duellist, Gustave de Borda; Reynaldo Hahn came too. Both men fired, and neither was hurt. The matter ended there. Proust's friends were surprised by his calm courage that day. In 1894 a Jewish army officer, Alfred Dreyfus, was wrongly found guilty of selling secrets to Germany. The fight over his case, called the Dreyfus affair, split France in two for years. On 13 January 1898 the novelist Émile Zola published his famous open letter J'accuse...! ("I accuse...!") in the newspaper L'Aurore, defending Dreyfus. Proust and his friends had already been at work for weeks. They were collecting signatures from writers and thinkers for a protest text asking for a new trial. It appeared in L'Aurore just after Zola's letter. Anatole France signed. Proust later said, with some pride, that he had been the first "Dreyfusard". His own father refused to sign. Adrien Proust, like most of official France, believed Dreyfus was guilty. After his sons put their names to the protest, he did not speak to them for a week. Proust went to the court every day during Zola's trial in February 1898, arriving in the morning with sandwiches and a small flask of coffee and staying until five in the afternoon. He watched the faces, the lies, the courage of Colonel Picquart. He wrote these scenes into his early novel Jean Santeuil. Much later, the Dreyfus affair became one of the great subjects of In Search of Lost Time. It shows how the affair broke friendships and changed the salons. From 1895 Proust worked in secret on a long novel about a young man named Jean Santeuil. He began it during a seaside holiday at Beg-Meil, in Brittany, with Reynaldo Hahn. The novel drew heavily on his own life: his childhood, his mother, his life in society, the Dreyfus affair. But it already changed and combined real events. He wrote hundreds and hundreds of pages. But the manuscript stayed unfinished and loosely organized. Around 1899 he gave it up, unhappy. The pages stayed in boxes for half a century. Jean Santeuil was finally published in 1952, thirty years after Proust's death. Readers found in it many first drafts of the great novel. In 1897, in a French magazine article, Proust discovered a new master: the English art critic John Ruskin, who had taught people how to look at cathedrals, at paintings, at nature. In December 1899 he wrote to a young English friend, Marie Nordlinger, that he was now at work on something quite new for him, about Ruskin and certain cathedrals. Ruskin died on 20 January 1900. Within days Proust published articles about him. Then he set out on "Ruskin pilgrimages": trips to see the cathedrals Ruskin had loved, at Rouen, Amiens, and elsewhere. In May 1900 Proust went to Venice with his mother, following Ruskin's books about the city. Reynaldo Hahn and Marie Nordlinger were waiting for them there. He went back alone in October of the same year. Venice stayed in his memory as a dream of stone and water. It later fills some beautiful chapters of the novel. That same October the family left boulevard Malesherbes for a new flat at 45 rue de Courcelles. Proust's English was limited. Even so, he decided to translate Ruskin into French. His mother wrote out first drafts for him. Marie Nordlinger checked the details. His translation of Ruskin's The Bible of Amiens (La Bible d'Amiens) came out in February 1904. His translation of Sesame and Lilies (Sésame et les lys) followed in 1906. For it he wrote a long and important preface about reading, first printed in the review La Renaissance latine on 15 June 1905 as "Sur la lecture" ("On Reading") and later called Journées de lecture ("Days of Reading"). The scholar Adam Watt sees this preface as a seed of the whole novel: the child reading in a garden, and the hours of reading as time both lost and saved, are already there. These years of patient work were his real school. Translating Ruskin taught him to build long sentences and to think about art, memory, and time. On 24 November 1903 Adrien Proust was struck by a brain hemorrhage at the medical school, where he had gone to lead a doctoral exam. He never woke again. He died on 26 November 1903. A huge crowd of doctors and officials followed his coffin to Père Lachaise Cemetery in Paris. Marcel dedicated his translation of The Bible of Amiens to his father's memory. Two years later he lost his mother. At the very start of September 1905 Jeanne Proust traveled with Marcel to the spa town of Évian. As soon as they arrived she was struck by violent attacks of uremia, a poisoning of the blood from failing kidneys, the same illness that had killed her own mother. She was brought back to Paris and refused most food and care. She died on 26 September 1905. She had never left the Jewish faith of her parents, so there was no church service. Her burial at Père Lachaise, on 28 September, was a civil one. The loss overwhelmed him. He had lived with his mother for thirty-four years. She had been his nurse, his first reader, his closest friend. In December 1905 he entered a clinic at Boulogne-sur-Seine, near Paris, run by Doctor Sollier, to treat his nerves. The cure did little, and he left after about six weeks. His grief, and the memory of his mother, later became central to his writing: the dead mother, and the pain of losing her, stand at the heart of In Search of Lost Time. At the end of 1906, after months spent in a hotel at Versailles, Proust moved into a flat at 102 boulevard Haussmann in Paris. He was installed there on 27 December 1906. The flat had belonged to his great-uncle Louis Weil, the same uncle in whose Auteuil house he was born; Proust and his brother each now owned a quarter of the building. His mother had often dined there, and Proust chose as his bedroom the very room where the old uncle had died. He said he could not bear to live in a home his mother had never known, even though the noisy street was bad for his asthma. To protect himself from noise, in 1910 he had the walls of his bedroom covered with plates of cork, a soft bark that stops sound. His housekeeper said that entering the room felt like walking into the inside of a giant bottle cork. In this brown, silent room he lived the other way round. He slept by day. He woke in the late afternoon. He worked all night, in bed, by the light of one small lamp. He loved music but could rarely go out to hear it. So, from early 1911, he paid for the "théâtrophone", a service that sent live opera down the telephone line. Lying in bed, he listened this way to whole operas, among them Debussy's Pelléas et Mélisande. From 1907 Proust spent his summers at the Grand Hôtel of Cabourg, a seaside town in Normandy. Proust believed the sea air was good for his chest. From his room, and in the dining hall, he watched the rich guests, the young girls on the beach, the waiters, the little dramas of hotel life. All this became Balbec, the seaside town of the novel, with its Grand Hotel and its "little band" of girls on the sea front. To visit friends along the coast, Proust hired motor taxis from a company run by his old school friend Jacques Bizet. One of the drivers was Alfred Agostinelli, a nineteen-year-old born in Monaco to an Italian family, who drove a red taxi. Proust liked him at once. In November 1907 Proust published an article in Le Figaro about these car trips, called "Impressions de route en automobile". In it, the church towers of Caen seem to dance and change places as the car turns. This moving picture later became the famous page about the three steeples of Martinville in the novel. The years 1908 and 1909 changed everything. Slowly, out of many small projects, the great novel took shape. First came the pastiches. A pastiche is a text written on purpose in the style of another writer. In early 1908, in Le Figaro, Proust retold a small news story, the Lemoine diamond fraud, in the styles of Balzac, Flaubert, and other great authors. Readers loved these games. They showed his perfect ear for style. In May 1908 he listed his projects in a letter to a friend: a study on the French nobility, a Paris novel, an essay on the critic Sainte-Beuve and on Flaubert, an essay on women, an essay on homosexuality, studies on stained-glass windows and on tombstones. All these pieces were about to melt into one single work. That same year he filled about seventy-five very large sheets of paper with scenes drawn from his own past: the evenings at Combray, the two family walks, the young girls by the sea, Venice. All these scenes later entered the novel. The sheets, known today as the "Soixante-quinze feuillets" ("Seventy-five sheets"), then disappeared into private hands for decades; they were only published in 2021. They are the oldest large piece of In Search of Lost Time that we have. Then came the plan of an essay against Sainte-Beuve. Sainte-Beuve had judged books by the life of the author: his friends, his manners, his talk. Proust believed the opposite. A book comes from a deeper self, another "I", that friends never meet. This essay, Contre Sainte-Beuve ("Against Sainte-Beuve"), was written in 1908 and 1909 but never finished. It was only published in 1954. In the draft opening of this essay, Proust presented an episode as something that had happened to him. One cold day his cook offered him a cup of tea, a drink he never took. By chance she brought some slices of dry toast with it. He dipped a piece of toast in the tea, and at the first taste, without warning, the summers of his childhood came back to him, whole and alive. Here, in the shape of a piece of toast, is the first version of the madeleine. Michael Wood points out how much Proust insists on chance in this scene: such a resurrection of the past can never be planned, only given. In a notebook of 1908 he also wrote about the uneven stones of the floor of Saint Mark's in Venice, another memory of this kind. And he asked himself, in writing, whether he should make a novel or a philosophy book, and whether he was a novelist at all. The answer came in 1909. The essay turned into a story. The story grew. By the end of the year, Proust was writing the childhood chapters of Combray. From 1909 to 1912 Proust wrote without rest. He filled school notebooks with his fast, hard-to-read handwriting. He glued extra strips of paper into the pages when there was no room left. At first he thought the novel would make one book of 800 or 900 pages. Soon it passed 1,200 pages, and it kept growing. He tried different titles. For a time he thought of calling the whole work Les Intermittences du cœur ("The Intermittences of the Heart"), that is, the stops and starts of feeling. In the end he chose À la recherche du temps perdu, "in search of lost time". Finding a publisher was long and painful. Between 1912 and 1913, the biggest houses of Paris all said no. The publisher Fasquelle asked a reader for a report on the manuscript. The reader wrote that after more than seven hundred pages he still had no idea what the book was about or where it was going. Fasquelle refused. The young Nouvelle Revue Française (NRF), the house of André Gide and Gaston Gallimard, said no on 23 December 1912; Fasquelle's refusal arrived the very next day. Gide had barely looked at the manuscript. He remembered Proust as a society snob, and he was put off by a few odd sentences. The publisher Ollendorff refused too. Its director wrote to a friend that he could not understand why a man needed thirty pages to describe how he turns over in bed before falling asleep. At last a young, new publisher, Bernard Grasset, agreed to print the book. But there was a condition: Proust himself had to pay all the costs. He accepted at once. He only wanted the book to exist. The first volume was called Du côté de chez Swann (Swann's Way). Proust corrected the proofs so heavily, rewriting whole pages in the margins, that the printers had to set much of the book twice. He paid extra for this too. He dedicated the book to Gaston Calmette, the director of Le Figaro, who had long supported him. A few months later, in March 1914, Calmette was shot dead in his own office by the wife of the minister Joseph Caillaux, in one of the great scandals of the age. Just before publication, the newspaper Le Temps printed a long interview with Proust. In it he explained his ideas about time, memory, and the many selves inside one person. He also warned that the narrator who says "I" in the book is not himself. Swann's Way went on sale on 14 November 1913. A young woman named Céleste Albaret, the new wife of Proust's taxi driver, carried signed copies across Paris to his friends and to the newspapers. She did not yet know that she would spend the next nine years at his side. The reviews were mixed. Some critics praised the new voice. Others were lost. Henri Ghéon, in the NRF's own magazine, called the book the work of a man with too much free time, and compared its sentences to a huge net dragging everything up from the sea floor. Then, in January 1914, André Gide read the book at last. He wrote Proust a letter of apology that became famous. Refusing this novel, he said, was the worst mistake the NRF had ever made, and one of the great regrets of his life. The NRF now begged to publish the next volumes. In May 1913 Alfred Agostinelli, the young driver from Cabourg, had come back into Proust's life. He had no work. Proust took him in as a secretary, to type the novel. Agostinelli moved into the flat with his companion, Anna. Proust fell deeply in love with him. It was a painful, jealous, impossible love. Agostinelli, a free spirit who dreamed of flying machines, felt like a prisoner in the dark flat. On 1 December 1913, two weeks after Swann's Way appeared, Agostinelli ran away with Anna to the south of France. Proust was desperate. He sent a friend, Albert Nahmias, to Monaco with money and secret offers for Agostinelli's father, to bring the young man back. The mission failed. According to Jean-Yves Tadié, Agostinelli probably did return to Paris for a few weeks at the start of 1914, brought back this time by the driver Odilon Albaret, before leaving again for good in April. In the south, Agostinelli joined a flying school near Antibes. As a pilot he took a new name: "Marcel Swann", from his old master and his old master's book. Proust, half forgiving, ordered a huge gift for him without telling him: an airplane worth 27,000 francs, and probably a Rolls-Royce car as well. Agostinelli refused the gifts. Proust even dreamed of having lines by his beloved poet Mallarmé painted on the machine. On 30 May 1914, on only his second flight alone, Agostinelli flew out over the sea against his teacher's orders. The plane fell into the water off Antibes. He could not swim. He drowned before help came. His last letter to Proust, full of joy about his flying, arrived after his death. Proust helped pay for divers to search for the body, which was found on 7 June, wearing a gold ring with the young man's initials, and he sent a large wreath of flowers for the grave. This death changed the novel. Proust's love for Agostinelli, and his grief after the young man's death, fed into the story of Albertine: the girl the narrator keeps almost as a prisoner, who runs away, and who dies in an accident. He even copied into the novel, almost word for word, a letter he had written to Agostinelli on the last morning of his life, about the plane and the car. It is the only letter between them that survives, found much later by the scholar Philip Kolb. Two months after Agostinelli's death, World War I began. Printing stopped. The second volume, already in proofs at Grasset, could not appear; the house of Grasset itself closed, its staff gone to the army. His brother Robert served as an army surgeon near the front. Close friends died in the fighting. Bertrand de Fénelon, whom Proust had deeply loved, was killed in battle on 17 December 1914, shot while leading his men; Proust only had sure news of it in March 1915. Gaston de Caillavet, the friend of his youth, died of illness in January of the same year. In the novel, the death of Saint-Loup at the front owes much to Fénelon. Proust himself, though far too sick for service, still had to appear before army medical boards, and was only declared unfit for good in 1916. He stayed in Paris through the air raids. He used the long, dark years to make the novel much bigger. Behind the cork walls he added many new characters, episodes, and themes, and the book grew from three planned volumes toward seven. In 1916 he finally moved from Grasset to the NRF, the house of Gaston Gallimard, which had once refused him and now wanted him badly. Gallimard's firm published all the rest of his work. During the war Proust also explored the hidden Paris of the night. He knew Albert Le Cuziat, who in 1917 opened a secret hotel for men at 11 rue de l'Arcade. Le Cuziat later gave some traits to Jupien in the novel. Céleste Albaret, in her memories, defended Proust against the darker stories told about these visits. She denied that he had given money to start the place, though she admitted that he had let Le Cuziat take a few pieces of old family furniture from storage. From 1913 Céleste Albaret, the driver's young wife, ran errands for Proust; from 1914, with the war emptying the household, she lived and worked in the flat as his housekeeper. For nine years, until his death, she was his cook, his nurse, his messenger, and his night-time listener. She learned his strange rules. Only one kind of coffee, from one shop, made drop by drop in a special filter. A croissant on a fixed saucer, brought only when he rang twice. Smoking powders burned in the room against his asthma, filling it with thick fumes. No perfume, no flowers, no noise, ever. She also kept his papers in order: the old notebooks, the new notebooks, the loose slips of paper covered with sudden ideas. She later told that during the war, on his orders, she burned thirty-two old black notebooks in the kitchen stove. It is one of the great losses of modern literature; some scholars think these notebooks may have held an early version of the later parts of the novel. Proust put pieces of Céleste into Françoise, the servant of the novel, together with two earlier servants, Félicie and Céline. Céleste herself said, half joking, that she had well deserved the title of his book The Captive. Fifty years later, in 1973, the old lady told her memories in a book, Monsieur Proust. It is one of the main sources about his daily life. In 1919 the building on boulevard Haussmann was sold, and Proust had to leave his cork-lined room. Before going, he burned old letters, private papers, and photographs he did not want to leave behind. He camped for some months in a furnished flat belonging to the actress Réjane, on the fourth floor of 8 bis rue Laurent-Pichat. Then, on 1 October 1919, he moved to his last home: a plain furnished flat on the fifth floor of 44 rue Hamelin. It was meant to be temporary. He died there. In June 1919 Gallimard published three of his books at the same time: the second volume of the novel, À l'ombre des jeunes filles en fleurs (Within a Budding Grove); a new edition of Swann's Way; and a collection called Pastiches et Mélanges. Slowly, talk of genius began to fill the salons and the papers. On 10 December 1919 the Prix Goncourt, the most famous book prize in France, went to Proust for À l'ombre des jeunes filles en fleurs. He won on the third round of voting, by six votes to four, against Roland Dorgelès, whose Les Croix de bois told the life of the soldiers in the trenches. Inside the small Goncourt academy, the writer Léon Daudet had led the campaign for Proust. Part of the press strongly attacked the choice. How could the prize go to a rich, sick society man of forty-eight, against a book about the war? Old soldiers protested. The socialist paper L'Humanité ran the headline "Place aux vieux !" ("Make way for the old!"), and another paper wrote about "electoral cooking". The young poet Louis Aragon called Proust a hard-working snob. The publisher of Dorgelès even printed a band around his book with the words "PRIX GONCOURT" in big letters and "four votes out of ten" in tiny ones. Gallimard took him to court and won. Jacques Rivière, the young editor of the NRF magazine, defended Proust in print. He argued that a revolution in art can also look backward, toward the classic study of the human heart. The scandal made Proust famous. On the evening of the prize, the men of the NRF, Gaston Gallimard and Jacques Rivière among them, were received in the bedroom of the rue Hamelin. In 1920 the French state gave him the Legion of Honour. Visitors, young writers, and translators now found their way up to the little flat of the rue Hamelin. Sick as he was, Proust now worked urgently to finish and publish his book. Le Côté de Guermantes I (The Guermantes Way I) came out at the end of October 1920. Le Côté de Guermantes II appeared together with Sodome et Gomorrhe I in one volume on 2 May 1921, printed in 8,000 copies. Sodome et Gomorrhe II followed on 29 April 1922, in three small volumes. Sodome et Gomorrhe spoke openly about homosexual love, both between men and between women. Some readers of the old world were shocked. André Gide, who wanted a prouder, more open way of writing about the subject, came several times to the rue Hamelin to argue about it through the fumes of the smoking powders. Gallimard also sold the rights for translations into English, German, and Spanish. In the spring of 1921 a Paris museum, the Jeu de Paume, opened a show of Dutch paintings. It included the View of Delft by Johannes Vermeer, which Proust had seen at The Hague in October 1902, during a journey with Bertrand de Fénelon, and had called the most beautiful painting in the world. One morning in May 1921, after a night without sleep, Proust asked the writer Jean-Louis Vaudoyer, whose articles on Vermeer he had admired, to take him there on his arm. That day the sick man saw the Vermeer, went on to a second exhibition, of paintings by Ingres, and even lunched at the Ritz. On the terrace beside the museum, someone photographed him in the sunlight; these are the last photographs of Proust. Proust told that he had felt a frightening dizziness on the stairs before going out. He gave that dizziness, and the painting, to a character in the novel: the old writer Bergotte rises from his sickbed to see the View of Delft, fixes his eyes on a little patch of yellow wall, tells himself that he should have written like that, and dies in front of the painting. It became one of the most famous death scenes in literature. Tadié warns, though, against the legend that Proust himself almost fainted before the Vermeer, a story spread later by his brother: Proust had invented Bergotte's illness weeks before the visit, and after the museum he calmly acted out his whole day for Céleste, with shining eyes. Proust had written Bergotte's death before that day; afterward he went back to the page and made it richer with what he had just felt. One day in the spring of 1922 Proust rang for Céleste. She saw at once that something had happened. He said to her: « Cette nuit, j'ai mis le mot "fin". » ("Last night, I wrote the word 'end'.") He added that now he could die. The book existed, from its first word to its last. Céleste placed this scene in the spring of 1922. His biographer William C. Carter thinks it may have happened years earlier, perhaps already in 1916, when Proust told his publisher that the whole novel was now written from beginning to end. In any case he went on correcting and adding until his last hours. But the frame of the book was now complete. On 18 May 1922 Proust went to a grand supper at the Hôtel Majestic, given by his English friends Sydney and Violet Schiff after the first night of Stravinsky's ballet Renard. Around the table sat Picasso, Stravinsky, the ballet director Diaghilev, and the Irish writer James Joyce, author of Ulysses. That same day, by a bad mistake, Proust had swallowed a dose of pure, undiluted adrenaline, which burned his throat and stomach; he went to the party all the same. For weeks afterward he could take almost nothing but ice cream and iced beer brought from the Ritz. Proust and Joyce then shared a taxi home. It did not go well. Joyce lit a cigarette and opened the window, both bad for Proust's lungs. Proust said politely that he had not read Joyce. Joyce answered that he had never read Proust. Céleste said the meeting left no mark at all on Proust; he never even mentioned Joyce's name at home. In early October 1922 Proust caught cold after going out to a party. The cold was followed by bronchitis, an inflammation of the airways in the lungs. He refused almost all treatment.

Marcel Paquet (21 February 1947 – 22 November 2014) was a Belgian philosopher. He was known for his philosophy on ontology, Belgian political philosophy, and on esthetics. Paquet was born in Charleroi, Belgium. Paquet died in Poznań, Poland, aged 67.

Marcel Paul Herriot (18 May 1934 – 14 September 2017) was a Roman Catholic bishop. He was born in Moussey, Vosges, France. Herriot was ordained to the priesthood in 1960. He served bishop of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Verdun, France, from 1987 to 1999. He then served as bishop of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Soissons from 1999 to 2008. Herriot died on 14 September 2017 in Saint-Dié-des-Vosges, Vosges, France at the age of 83.

Marcel Mauss (May 10, 1872 - February 10, 1950) was a French anthropologist and sociologist. With a strong background in sociology, he began using ethnography to look at how different cultures build relationships. He was also influenced by his uncle, another famous anthropologist, Émile Durkheim. Mauss is known for his work on gifts and exchange, magic, sacrifice, the body, and comparing cultures. Mauss’s most famous work is The Gift. The Gift is about the ways gifts and exchanges build relationships. Mauss is also known for influencing structural anthropologists such as Claude Lévi-Strauss. Marcel Mauss was born in Épinal, France in 1872. His parents were Gerson Mauss and Rosine (Durkheim) Mauss. He was raised in a non-observant Jewish family. In the early 1890s, Mauss went to the University of Bordeaux where he studied many subjects including religion and philosophy. Later he moved to Paris, France where he studied at the École Pratique des Hautes Études (an important French research school). In Paris, Mauss studied Sanskrit, Hebrew, history of religion, and other topics. Mauss eventually became a professor at École Pratique des Hautes Études. He taught about many different religions. During World War I, Mauss served in the French army as an interpreter. Mauss helped form the Institut d'ethnologie (Ethnology Institute) at the University of Paris in 1925 with Paul Rivet and Lucien Lévy-Bruhl. He also was the chair of the sociology department at the Université de Paris from 1931-1939. Mauss’ theories about the role of gifts in Māori culture relied heavily on the information provided by Tamati Ranapiri. Ranapiri was a Māori scholar who exchanged letters with ethnographer Elsdon Best. Through these letters, Ranapiri explained how gifts were used to connect people in Māori society. According to Ranapiri, gifts created commitment without force. These commitments created by gifts made social relationships and bonds stronger. Elsdon Best was an ethnographer who studied the Māori people of New Zealand. Mauss used Best’s letters and primary data to write his work about Māori gift giving. Émile Durkheim was Marcel Mauss’ uncle as well as a professional influence. Mauss was Durkheim's nephew, student, and collaborator. The two worked together on many projects. Durkheim and Mauss worked together to publish the book Primitive Classifications. This book was a response to Immanuel Kant’s categories of understanding. Durkheim and Mauss also worked together to publish articles in L’Année Sociologique. L’Année Sociologique was a sociology journal created by Durkheim. Mauss referred to Hubert as his "Siamese twin" and they worked together on a couple works, such as Sacrifice: Its Nature and Functions (1899) and Outline of a General Theory of Magic (1904). In works that they are not co-authored, they cite each other. As Mauss said "[e]verything I don't know, Mauss knows, and everything Mauss doesn't know, I know." Their major works and theories were products of their teamwork, and therefore both greatly influenced each other. Primitive Classifications, an essay by both Mauss and Durkheim, was published in Durkheim’s sociology journal, Année Sociologique in 1903. In 1963 the essay was translated into English by Rodney Needham. Then British and American anthropologists could read the essay. In Primitive Classifications, Durkheim and Mauss write about categories of human thought, including time and space. They said that those categories come from societies we live in, not the individual mind. Durkheim and Mauss used data from tribal societies, such as the Zuni and the Sioux, to make their point in this essay. This essay inspired the work of a number of contemporary or near-contemporary social scientists, including Rodney Needham, Mary Douglas, Steven Lukes, Claude Levi-Strauss, Basil Bernstein, and Barry Schwartz. Techniques of the Body was a lecture given by Mauss in 1934 at a Société de Psychologie meeting. It was then published in the Journal de psychologie normal et patholigique in 1935. In this essay, Mauss’ theories of techniques of the body focused on how various techniques such as running, walking, and birthing are similar and different across societies. He argued that each society develops their own habits and that there is a social concept of “habitus”. He defines habitus as the learned habits of people that are different across individuals but also can be different across societies, educations, and fashions. In his essay, Mauss states that techniques of the body do vary by age and sex. He believes that there is a division of techniques in younger and older people, as well as in males and females. The Gift was published in 1925. It was written partially in response to the Bolshevik Revolution. In this book, Mauss argued that every society has both markets and money of some kind as well as altruism. Mauss claims that gifts are a “total social fact” which have spiritual parts to them. The Gift also examines gift giving traditions of some indigenous peoples. Mauss writes about the Māori idea of “Hau." He also talks about Potlatch, which was first practiced by indigenous groups in North America. Mauss believed that gift giving can tell us a lot about social relationships. He also believed that gift giving was connected to power. Mauss claimed that there is no such thing as a free gift. He thought every gift was part of an ongoing system of giving and receiving. Mauss saw sacrifice as a system of exchange as well. In 1899, Mauss published Sacrifice: Its Nature and Functions with Henri Hubert. This book compares many religious practices with a focus on sacrifice and the body. Mauss and Hubert compared religions from many places and time periods. They describe sacrifice as a system which involves both actions that are aimed towards a holy person or object and actions that are aimed away from a holy person or object. Mauss and Hubert claimed that the body is the result of many different habits and qualities. They claimed that a person is made up of certain actions that are performed through specific behaviors. Mauss teamed up with Hubert again in 1902 to publish A General Theory of Magic. In this book, Mauss and Hubert claimed that social events, rather than individual people, were magic. This is another cross-cultural comparison, like Mauss and Hubert's work on sacrifice. They claim that magic is a social experience. The book examines the relationships between magic and religion, science, and technology. Mauss and Hubert also trace the long-lasting impact of magic on our modern ideas, such as the idea of good and bad luck. Manual of Ethnography is a collection of Mauss's lectures on how to successfully do ethnography. Ethnography is when sociologists and anthropologists try to understand a culture through observing and sometimes participating in that group. In his lectures, he shows that observers should not assume that a culture will have the same opinions and ways of doing things as their own culture. He also describes how ethnographers should observe, collect data, and how to understand the different social structures that make up a group. Saints, Heroes, Myths, and Rites is a collection of essays written by Mauss, Hubert and Hertz. Like Durkheim, they believed that as people started practicing their own religions, people would find new ways to maintain a sense of community based on their shared morals. Myths are also part of religion. They are a result of any human society. Because they are found in every society, they are not imaginary. Myths are subconscious symbols that the individual uses to understand their experiences. The subconscious is also called the unconscious. It is the part of a person's mind that thinks and remembers things without the person knowing it. In 2017, Georgina Stewart published a criticism of The Gift, specifically on Mauss' understanding of Hau. Stewart claims that a misunderstanding of Māori beliefs about the cosmos and language differences caused Mauss to misunderstand the Māori concept of Hau. Alain Testart (1998) claimed that Mauss exaggerated the idea that all gifts need to be repaid. Testart said that there were some truly free gifts, such as giving money to a homeless person as you walk by them. James Laidlaw also points out an example of free gifts within Jainism, a religion where followers believe that they cause a war between microorganisms if they prepare their own food, so they rely on outside food donations. Mauss is credited for being a major inspiration for Claude Lévi-Strauss and Pierre Bourdieu. Claude Lévi-Strauss went on to develop the structuralist view of cultural anthropology. Mauss is also known for inspiring future work on exchange theory and economic anthropology. Mauss' cross-cultural comparisons were radical for his time, and he helped establish a foundation for the next generation of cultural anthropologists to use a similar comparative approach. Mauss' The Gift inspired French philosopher Georges Bataille in his ideas of excess energy and waste of this energy in societies. Mauss' influence has also appeared in French sociologist, Pierre Bourdieu's works. In them, Bourdieu highlight's Mauss' idea of habitus. Habitus describes habits and skills that we learn while being within our society. These are fixed habits within us and influence the way we perceive and react to the world around us. Someone with a similar upbringing might have similar habitus.

Marcelina Almeida (around 1830–1880) was a writer from Uruguay. She lived in Montevideo since she was young. Almeida used the names 'Abel' and 'Reine mi bella acclamada' (an anagram of her full name) for her writings. Her book, Por una fortuna una cruz, is known as the first Uruguayan feminist novel. Marcelina Almeida, also known as Marcelina Almeida Abel, was born around 1830 in Argentina. Her exact birth and death dates are unknown. In a poem, Francisco Acuña de Figueroa described her as a Uruguayan by adoption, born in Argentina. Almeida's romantic novel Por una fortuna una cruz was published in Montevideo in 1860. It talks about "the forced marriage of a fifteen-year-old girl with a twenty-five-year-old man". The book started a big debate in Montevideo's newspapers. People discussed the book's quality and the fact that a woman questioned marriage. Almeida faced personal attacks, many under fake names. Virginia Cánova, a researcher, explained that Almeida supported liberal feminism, talking about women's lack of rights and how they were always seen as minors under men's protection. She criticized forced marriages, where the father decides for the daughter. In 1991, Cánova found a copy of the novel in the National Library of Uruguay, reviving works missing from Uruguayan literary history. This allowed a limited reissue of the book, along with a study about "The origins of feminism in Uruguay." The study shows that feminism began in the early 19th century and not in the early 20th century, as previously thought. Female writers like Almeida, not María Eugenia Vaz Ferreira and Delmira Agustini, were the pioneers. 8 Almeida also wrote poems, a short story, and articles between 1860-61 for the Semanario Uruguayo and poems for the literary magazine La Aurora de Montevideo between 1862 and 1863. Almeida died around 1880.

Marcel Cornelis van den Dop with artist name Marcello (1954 – 14 January 2025) was a Dutch artist. Van den Dop was born in Leiden in 1954. He studied at the Gerrit Rietveld Academy in Amsterdam. From 1990 he formed an artist duo together with Els Meesche, who later became his wife. They made hundreds of drawings, paintings and silkscreen prints; often about rock stars. They were the owner of Rock Gallery (formerly named Galerie Haags) in The Hague. Due to the rise of digital printing techniques, they decided to fully focus on art. They also came up with artistic projects. With pencil and pen he made football collection cards of the footballers of ADO Den Haag; and other artistic projects includes the yellow-green “Den Hagelslag” (a Dutch pun on hagelslag and The Hague); they initiated the exposition “Rembrandt2000”; Mesdag Revisited and Radar Love. In 2016 Van den Dop started “Rock History Tour”, a bus tour in The Hague along important pop history places. Van den Dop died from an illness on 14 January 2025, at the age of 70.

Marcelo Hilario del Pilar y Gatmaitan (August 30, 1850 – July 4, 1896), was a leading propagandist of the Philippine Revolution in 1896. Marcelo H. del Pilar was born in Cupang (now Barangay San Nicolas), Bulacan, on August 30, 1850, to parents Julián del Pilar and Blasa Gatmaytan. He studied at the Colegio de San José and later at the University of Santo Tomas, where he finished his law course in 1880. In 1882, del Pilar founded the nationalist newspaper Diariong Tagalog (Tagalog Newspaper). He organized various anti-friar demonstrations while in the Philippines. He also wrote anti-friar pamphlets like the Dasalan at Tocsohan, Caiigat Cayo, etc. Del Pilar went to Spain in 1888 to escape persecution by the Spanish authorities. He became the second editor of La Solidaridad (Solidarity) in Madrid. Publication of the La Solidaridad stopped in 1895 due to lack of money. Del Pilar decided to return to the Philippines to lead a revolution against Spain. However, he cancelled his trip due to his illness. Del Pilar died of tuberculosis in Barcelona on July 4, 1896, a pauper, away from his wife and 2 children.

Marcello Malpighi (10 March 1628 – 29 November 1694) was an Italian doctor, who gave his name to several physiological features, like the Malpighian tubule system. Although the microscope was invented early in the 17th century, it was not much used until Robert Hooke improved the instrument. Then Marcello Malpighi, Hooke, Nehemiah Grew and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek had a virtually untried tool in their hands as they began their investigations. Working on frogs and extrapolating to humans, Malpighi demonstrated the structure of the lungs, previously thought to be a homogeneous mass of flesh, and he offered an explanation for how air and blood mixed in the lungs. Malpighi also used the microscope for his studies of the skin, kidneys, and liver. For example, after he dissected the body of a black man, Malpighi made some groundbreaking headway into the origin of black skin. He found that the black pigment was associated with a layer of mucus just beneath the skin. He was the first to see capillaries in animals, and he discovered the link between arteries and veins. He may have been the first person to see this under a microscope. The microscope let Malpighi discover that the silk worm does not use lungs to breathe, but small holes in their skin called spiracles. This turned out to be true of all insects. Because Malpighi had a wide knowledge of both plants and animals, and he made contributions to the study of both. The Royal Society in London published two volumes of his botanical and zoological works in 1675 and 1679. Another edition followed in 1687, and a supplementary volume in 1697. In his autobiography, Malpighi speaks of his Anatome Plantarum, decorated with the engravings of Robert White (1645–1703) as "the most elegant format in the whole literate world".

Marcello Giordani (born Marcello Guagliardo; 25 January 1963 – 5 October 2019) was an Italian operatic tenor. He sang leading roles of the Italian and French repertoire in opera houses throughout Europe and the United States. He worked with the New York Metropolitan Opera, where he sang in over 240 performances from the time of his debut there in 1993. He founded the Marcello Giordani Foundation to help young opera singers. Giordani died on 5 October 2019 in Augusta, Sicily from a heart attack at the age 56.

Marcello Gandini (26 August 1938 – 13 March 2024) was an Italian automotive designer mostly famous of Lamborghini sports cars designing. He was born in Turin, in the family of a wealthy aristocrat. The father owned a pharmaceutical company. After graduating from school, he started setting up sports cars. In the early sixties, he became acquainted with Nuccio Bertone, who later offered him to work with a designer in the car studio Bertone. In 1980, he left Bertone to start his freelance designer's career. Since 1990, he works only in small projects. He designed Lamborghini Miura and Countach (1973), Fiat X1/9, BMW 5 Series, Lancia Stratos and many others. Gandini died on 13 March 2024, at the age of 85.

Marcelo Alberto Bonelli (Born, October 8, 1955) is an Argentine political and economics journalist. He began his career in 1985 on El Trece. Since 2005 he has been the host of the morning news show Arriba Argentinos on Channel 13. He writes for the newspaper Clarín. He is a fan of Racing Club. He has been awarded national and international prizes on various occasions: in 1997 he received the Konex Prize. In 1998 he received the Ondas Prize, awarded by Cadena Ser of Spain for the investigation carried out in the program A Dos Voces on the disappeared children in Argentina. On March 17, 2017, the newspaper Clarín published an article by Bonelli in which he stated that, during an interview between the former president of the Spanish government Felipe González and President Mauricio Macri, the former had told him that "no one is going to invest seriously in Argentina until Cristina's acts of corruption are judged and sentenced", after asking "When is Cristina going to go to jail?". The former president responded by sending González and Macri two notes. He urged them to confirm what was stated in Bonelli's article, and considering that the Argentine president had the duty to reject demonstrations that "import unprecedented extortion and undue interference in internal affairs, in addition to the exclusive recourse of justice." That day, González denied through his spokesman that the former President had maintained that position before the Argentine President, news that was published by the newspaper in a note by Bonelli himself, in which he insisted that what he had published was true. In the same sense, Felipe González spoke and asked the newspaper to clarify the situation, which the newspaper did not.

Marcelo Spina (born July 23, 1970) is an Argentinean-American architect (AIA) and educator. He is a partner in Los Angeles-based architecture firm PATTERNS, which he founded in 2002. Since 2001, he has been a Design and Applied Studies Faculty at SCI-Arc. He holds a B.Arch. from the National University of Rosario, Argentina (1994) and a Master in Advanced Architectural Design from the Graduate School of Architecture, Planning and Preservation of Columbia University in New York (1997). Spina has worked for RUR Architects and Keller Easterling in New York and Gerardo Caballero Architects. He opened his own office Banchini + Spina Arquitectos in Rosario, Argentina (1998-2002). At SCI-Arc, he was the coordinator of the Applied Studies Program from 2005 to 2009 and the Architectural Technologies Postgraduate Program from 2011 to 2019. He has been a member of the Board of Trustees since 2016. He has served on national juries and advisory boards such as The Architectural League of New York, Progressive Architecture Awards and the Mies Crown Hall Americas Prize. He has been a visiting professor at the Universities of Pennsylvania, Syracuse, Harvard, Berkeley, Vienna, Innsbruck, and Di Tella among others. In 2013, he was the Louis I. Kahn visiting assistant professor of Architectural Design at Yale University School of Architecture. Spina is the co-author of PATTERNS Embedded (ACDCU, 2010), Material Beyond Materials (SCI-Arc Press 2012) and Mute Icons and other Dichotomies of the Real in Architecture (Princeton 2016). He co-curated Matters of Sensation at Artists Space with Georgina Huljich.
