He was the president of PEN International from 1947 to 1949. He died in Nice on 6 May 1949 after suffering a heart attack.

Maurice Bernard Sendak (June 10, 1928 – May 8, 2012) was an American writer and illustrator of children's literature. He was best known for his book Where the Wild Things Are, which was released in 1963. Sendak was born on June 10, 1928 in Brooklyn, New York City. His parents were Sadie (née Schindler) and Philip Sendak. Sendak was a homosexual and had a partner Dr. Eugene Glynn from 1957 until 2007 when Glynn died. Sendak died on May 8, 2012 in his home in Danbury, Connecticut from a stroke. He was 83 years old. His remains were cremated.

Maurice Ralph Hilleman (August 30, 1919 – April 11, 2005) was an American microbiologist. He specialized in vaccinology. He developed over 36 vaccines, more than any other scientist. Of the 14 vaccines currently recommended, he developed eight: those for measles, mumps, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, chickenpox, meningitis, pneumonia and Haemophilus influenza bacteria. He also played a role in the discovery of the cold-producing adenoviruses, the hepatitis viruses, and the cancer-causing virus SV40. He is credited with saving more lives than any other medical scientist of the 20th century. Robert Gallo described him as "the most successful vaccinologist in history". At the time of his death on April 11, 2005, at the age of 85, Hilleman was Adjunct Professor of Pediatrics at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia. Hilleman was a forceful man who was at the same time modest in his claims. None of his vaccines or discoveries are named after him. He ran his laboratory like a military unit, and he was the one in command He terminated every subordinate who did not measure up to his standards. For a time, he kept a row of "shrunken heads" (actually fakes made by one of his children) in his office as trophies that represented each of his fired employees. He used profanity and tirades freely to drive his arguments home, and once, famously, refused to attend a mandatory "charm school" course intended to make Merck middle managers more civil. His men were fiercely loyal to him. Hilleman was an elected member of the US National Academy of Science, the Institute of Medicine, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and the American Philosophical Society. In 1988 President Ronald Reagan presented him with the National Medal of Science, the nation's highest scientific honor. He received the Prince Mahidol Award from the King of Thailand for the advancement of public health, as well as a special lifetime achievement award from the World Health Organization, the Mary Woodard Lasker Award for Public Service and the Sabin Gold Medal and Lifetime Achievement Awards. Robert Gallo, co-discoverer of the virus that causes AIDS, once said "If I had to name a person who has done more for the benefit of human health, with less recognition than anyone else, it would be Maurice Hilleman. Maurice should be recognized as the most successful vaccinologist in history". After Hilleman's death Ralph Nader wrote, "Yet almost no one knew about him, saw him on television, or read about him in newspapers or magazines. His anonymity, in comparison with Madonna, Michael Jackson, Jose Canseco, or an assortment of grade B actors, tells something about our society's and media's concepts of celebrity; much less of the heroic." On October 15, 2008, Merck named its Durham, North Carolina vaccine manufacturing facility in memory of Hilleman.

Sir Maurice Flanagan [[Order of the British Empire (17 October 1928 – 7 May 2015) was a British businessman. He was the founding CEO of Emirates. He was also the Executive Vice-Chairman of The Emirates Group. Flanagan was born in Leigh, Lancashire. He was married to Audrey Bolton from 1955 until his death. They had three children. He lived in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. Flanagan died on 7 May 2015 in London, aged 86.

Maurice Green (May 5, 1926 – December 5, 2017) was an American virologist. His research career spanned more than 60 years. He was thought as a pioneer in the study of animal viruses, in particular their role in cancer. Green founded the Institute of Molecular Virology at St. Louis University School of Medicine in the late 1950s, and served as its Chairman until his death in 2017. He was born in New York City. Green died in St. Louis, Missouri on December 5, 2017 of natural causes at the age of 91.

Maurice Marie Jean Pon (26 October 1921 – 3 April 2019) was a French lyricist. He was best known for his work with Henri Salvador. He also wrote for artists such as Bourvil, Fernandel, Jean Sablon, André Claveau and Les Frères Jacques. He was born in Bordeaux. Pon died on 3 April 2019 in Île-de-France. He was 97.

Maurice Sanford Fox (October 11, 1924 – January 26, 2020) was an American geneticist and molecular biologist. He was professor Emeritus of Biology at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he was department chair between 1985 and 1989. He was important for the creation of the Council for a Livable World. Fox died on January 26, 2020 at the age of 95.

Maurice Rajsfus (9 April 1928 – 13 June 2020) was a French writer, journalist and historian. He was the author of many books talking about the themes such as the Jewish genocide in France, the police, and attacks on civil rights. In 1994 he co-founded the "Observatory of Public Liberties" ("l'Observatoire des libertés publiques"), which he led.

Maurice Petty (March 27, 1939July 25, 2020) was an American NASCAR crew chief and engine builder. He worked for Petty Enterprises, of which he was part owner. He was added into the International Motorsports Hall of Fame in 2011. He was honored into the NASCAR Hall of Fame in 2014. He was the first engine builder to be honored in that Hall. Petty was born in Randolph County, North Carolina. Petty was the younger brother of Richard Petty. Petty died on the morning of July 25, 2020, at the age of 81.

Maurice Houdayer (18 July 1931 – 1 October 2020) was a French rower. He competed at the 1956 European Rowing Championships in Bled, Yugoslavia, with the men's eight where they won the silver medal. He was part of the 1956 Summer Olympics in Melbourne with the men's eight, finishing in eighth place. Houdayer died on 1 October 2020 at the age of 89.

Maurice Malleret (30 September 1931 – 3 October 2021) was a French writer, historian, musicologist, and poet. He worked with the magazine La Vie du rail and Cercle Littéraire des Écrivains Cheminots. He was a member of the Société des poètes et artistes de France. He was born in Cosne-d'Allier, France. He also worked at the National Museum of Natural History, France. Malleret died on 3 October 2021 in Lavault-Sainte-Anne, France from congestive heart failure, aged 90.

Maurice Grosser (October 23, 1903 – December 22, 1986) was an American painter, art critic, and writer. He was the longtime companion of Virgil Thomson. Maurice Grosser was born on October 23, 1903, in Huntsville, Alabama. He designed the scenery for two operas by Virgil Thomson: Four Saints in Three Acts (1934) and The Mother of Us All (1947). Grosser died on December 22, 1986, in Manhattan. Paintings by Maurice Grosser are at the Museum of Modern Art, the Brooklyn Museum, the Smithsonian American Art Museum, and the Huntsville Museum of Art.

Maurizio Giuliano (born 1975) is an Italian journalist, writer and traveller. In 2004, he was in the Guinness Book of World Records as the youngest person who has been to all the countries in the world. In 2006/2007, he worked for the UN. Maurizio Giuliano was born on 24 February 1975 in Milan, Italy, with a lawyer as a father and a housewife as a mother. He lived in Cuba, Chile, and Indonesia, among other countries. As of 2004, he knew eight languages according to one source, while another source specified that he "spoke" five and had a "passion" for two more. He went to school in Milan and Manchester, and then studied at the University of Oxford in 1996 and the University of Cambridge in 1997. At Oxford, he studied at University College to know about Oxford's inter-disciplinary course in Philosophy, Politics, and Economics (PPE), especially Latin America and eastern Europe. As of 1998, he was a research fellow at the Centre for Social Studies (CESOC) in Santiago, Chile. He wrote two books and some articles on Cuban politics, especially on the US embargo (which usually stops Americans from doing business with Cubans), which he thinks (in the book "La Transición Cubana y el "Bloqueo" Norteamericano" and other works) is not good. In an article published in the British academic journal Democratization in 1998, he focused in particular on how the US embargo against Cuba helps create "empathy" by third parties towards Cuba, so that Cubans think it is support for Cuba's government. So he argued that the US Government – in addition to the embargo's direct influence on supporting Cuba's regime – indirectly interferes with the possibility of improving Cuba. That is because third countries, foreign non-governmental organizations and prominent individuals lend support to Cuba's resistance to the US embargo, and this offsets external pressures for democracy, thereby allowing the Cuban regime to convert such "empathy" into a source of legitimacy at home. His scholarly work on internal Cuban politics, notably on the 1996 purge of Havana's Centre for American Studies (CEA) (contained in the book "El Caso CEA" published in 1998), has been the object of academic reviews, as it exposed the internal conflicts between Cuba's political apparatus and the country's intelligentsia (most intelligent people), previously unknown. According to some reviews, the book, a work of investigative journalism helped by academic analysis, dealt a strong blow to hard-liners within the regime, by exposing for the first time the internal conflicts between Cuba's apparatus and its intelligentsia. In 2001, Cuban exiled scholars Alberto Álvarez and Gerardo González, who were among those purged from the CEA, wrote the book "¿ Intelectuales vs. Revolución ? El caso del Centro de Estudios sobre América", which strongly built upon Giuliano's book to offer further insights on relations between Cuba's political apparatus and the country's intellectuals. Besides work on Cuba, other countries Giuliano covered in his journalistic work include East Timor and Myanmar (formerly known as Burma). In 2000, he visited North Korea and published an essay about his visit, essentially describing his tour around the country as being like a movie made by the North Korean authorities. In his journalistic work, he reportedly ran into problems with the authorities of at least two countries. In 1998, he was denied entry to Myanmar after making contact with the National League for Democracy and taking photos of its leader Aung San Suu Kyi. And on 30 October 2002, he was reportedly detained and manhandled by Israeli authorities while crossing the Allenby Bridge. Giuliano's writings have also included lighter topics. During his time in Kabul, for example, he wrote restaurant reviews for a local English-language magazine. In the early 2000s, Giuliano was a consultant for the Italian Senate's Committee on Human Rights. At that time, at least some of his writings were also intended to influence the positions of the Italian Government on certain human rights issues, as was the case with material that he wrote on North Korea. In 2004, Giuliano worked for the International Organization for Migration in the elections for Afghan refugees in Pakistan, and in 2005 worked in Afghanistan for the United Nations Development Programme. In both cases, he was working in the field of communications with the media. Between 2006 and 2008, he served with the United Nations, again in the field of media relations, in the Central African Republic, and Cameroon following the refugee crisis caused by the battle of N'Djamena of February 2008. According to the Guinness Book, through his work, he had travelled to every single sovereign country in the world (which totalled 193 according to the Guinness Book) by 20 February 2004, aged 28 years and 361 days. He claimed that he had visited a total of up to 238 territories (including the 193 sovereign countries recognized by Guinness), and stated that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) had been the hardest country to get into, after numerous attempts and long waits to get a visa. He started travelling at age 14, and believes that, as of 2004, he had travelled at least two million miles, including on the Trans-Siberian Railway and through 11 round-the-world air journeys. Some of his earliest journeys were to Albania and Sierra Leone in 1991, aged 16, and to Mongolia in 1992 for their national festivities Naadam. Most of his later travels were related to his journalistic work. On 20 February 2004 he visited Suriname, thereby completing his visit to all sovereign nations of the world. He held a press conference there on 24 February, where he stated that he had chosen Suriname to complete his record, as the country had always fascinated him due to its richness and variety in cultures and ethnicities. He then travelled from Suriname to London, with 42 passports (of which 30 were Italian and 12 British) filled with immigration stamps, in order to prove his record to Guinness World Records. He claimed that most of his travels were unrelated to the record, and that only since 2001, on the suggestion of friends, did he have the Guinness Record in mind when planning his travels. In explaining his record, however, he stated that he might have an "addiction to crossing borders".

Maurizio Delvecchio (born 22 May 1962) is an Italian painter. He was born in Basel, Switzerland into an Italian family. Back in Italy, with his parents, he graduated from the Art School in Ravenna. In 1985 he graduated from the Academy of Fine Arts in Ravenna. He lives and works in Cesenatico (FC). He participated in the 54 Biennale of Art in Venice in 2011. Museo d'arte of Avellino (Italy) with Il Tramonto e l'attesa … (2013). Museo permanente di Arte Contemporanea of Amatrice (RI) (Italy).

Mauro Staccioli (11 February 1937 – 1 January 2018) was an Italian sculptor. He was born in Volterra, Italy. Staccioli started teaching and in 1968 joined the Academy of Fine Arts of Brera in Milan. In the beginning of the 1970s, his career began as his works were about urban environment and, with sculpture, tries to give answers to social questions. Among all his permanent work installations: Villa Celle in Santomato of Pistoia (1982); Olympic Park in Seoul (1988); Djerassi Foundation in Woodside (1987–1991); Museum of Contemporary Art of Seul Kwachon (1990); Museum of Contemporary Art of San Diego (1996); Ordino d’Arcalis in Andorra (1991); Munich (1996); Parc Tournay-Solvay in Brussels (1996); Villa Glori in Roma (1997); Schuman roundabout in Brussels (1998); Lapiz building in La Jolla (2003); Chiaopanshan International Sculpture Park in Taiwan (2003); University of Puerto Rico Arecibo (2004); Carrazeda de Ansiães in Portugal (2008); Centre Val St Quentin in Voisins-le-Bretonneux (2008). Staccioli died of complications from pneumonia on 1 January 2018 in Milan at the age of 80.

Maurizio Calvesi (18 September 1927 – 24 July 2020) was an Italian art critic, historian and essayist. He was born in Rome. He was a professor at the Sapienza University of Rome. He was also a member of Accademia dei Lincei. He wrote about art history during the Renaissance and Baroque times. Calvesi died on 24 July 2020 in Rome, aged 92.

Mauricio Simon Umansky (born June 25, 1970) is a real estate broker and television personality. He is the co-founder and CEO of The Agency RE, a real estate brokerage based in Beverly Hills, California. Since 2022, he has appeared on the Netflix reality series Buying Beverly Hills. Mauricio Umansky was born in Mexico City, Mexico, on June 25, 1970, to Eduardo Umansky, a clothing manufacturer, and Estella Sneider, a psychologist. He has a younger sister. He is of Jewish heritage, with Russian, Greek, and Turkish roots. Umansky had neutropenia as a child, which led to him spending significant time in the hospital and becoming legally blind in one eye. He attended the University of Southern California but left to start a business venture. Umansky founded a clothing company, 90265, in 1989 and claims to have started the trend of women wearing oversized T-shirts with leggings. He sold the company in 1996. Umansky started his real estate career at Hilton & Hyland, a firm co-owned by his brother-in-law, Richard Hilton. His first sale was a property in Brentwood, California, for $7.5 million. In 2011, he co-founded The Agency RE, a real estate brokerage in Beverly Hills. In 2018, he was ranked the third individual U.S. real estate agent for total sales transactions by RealTrends. Umansky, Billy Rose and Blair Chang co-founded The Agency RE, a global boutique real estate brokerage, based in Beverly Hills, in July 2011. Umansky was ranked as the third individual U.S. real estate agent for total number of real estate sales transactions in 2018 by RealTrends as published in The Wall Street Journal. Umansky made his TV debut in 2005 on the MTV series Newlyweds: Nick and Jessica. He has appeared as a guest on The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills since 2010. Since 2022, he has been a main cast member on Netflix's Buying Beverly Hills. He also competed in the 32nd season of Dancing with the Stars in 2023 with Emma Slater, and was the sixth couple eliminated. In April 2023, Umansky published The Dealmaker: How to Succeed in Business & Life Through Dedication, Determination & Disruption. Umansky lives in Encino, Los Angeles with his wife Kyle Richards, their three daughters, and their dogs. Umansky married actress Kyle Richards on January 20, 1996, and they have three daughters: Alexia, Sophia, and Portia Umansky. He is also stepfather to Richards' daughter from a previous marriage, Farrah Brittany. In July 2023, it was reported that Umansky and Richards had separated after 27 years of marriage. Umansky is a cousin of Doris Bessudo from Bravo's Mexican Dynasties. Umansky and his wife are part of the "First Families" of the Children's Hospital Los Angeles, having donated $100,000 or more. He is also on the board of Giveback Homes, which builds homes for families in need.

Maurice Richard "Maury" Povich (born January 17, 1939, Washington D.C., U.S.) is an American television talk show host. He hosted the tabloid talk show Maury, which began in 1991 and ended in 2022. Povich graduated from the Landon School in 1957. He graduated from the University of Pennsylvania in 1962 with a degree in television journalism. He hosted the 2000 revival of the television game show Twenty One. Povich is married to former news anchor Connie Chung.

Maxlei dos Santos Luzia or simply Max (27 February 1975 – 26 July 2017) was a Brazilian goalkeeper. He was born in Rio de Janeiro. He was known for playing for Portuguesa-RJ, Vila Nova and Botafogo. In June 2017, Max was the victim of an attempted robbery. The former goalkeeper suffered a fractured right hand and a cerebral edema. On 26 July 2017, Santos Luzia died of a cerebral edema in Rio de Janeiro at the age of 42.

Max Azria (Hebrew: מקס עזריה; Arabic: ماكس عزرية) (January 1, 1949 – May 6, 2019) was a Tunisian-American fashion designer. He founded the contemporary women's clothing brand BCBGMAXAZRIA. Azria was also the designer, chairman and CEO of the BCBG Max Azria Group. He was born Sfax, Tunisia. Azria died on May 6, 2019 in Houston, Texas from lung cancer at the age of 70.

Max Carl Friedrich Beckmann (February 12, 1884 – December 27, 1950) was a German painter. He is considered one of the most important expressionist painters, despite rejecting the term. After World War I, he was associated with the artistic movement New Objectivity, critical of the state of the country during the Weimar Republic. He left Germany for the Netherlands, in 1937, and moved to the United States, in 1947, where he would spent his final years.

Max Born (11 December 1882 – 5 January 1970) was a German-British Jewish physicist and mathematician who was important in the development of quantum mechanics. He also made contributions to solid-state physics and optics and supervised the work of a number of important physicists in the 1920s and 30s. Born became a British subject in 1939. He won the 1954 Nobel Prize in Physics. Born's descendants include his grandaughter Olivia Newton-John and his great-granddaughter Chloe Rose Lattanzi.

Max Ludwig Henning Delbrück (September 4, 1906 – March 9, 1981) was a German-American biophysicist and Nobel laureate. Delbrück was one of the most influential people in the movement of physical scientists into biology during the 20th century. Delbrück's big idea was to explore genetics by means of the bacteriophage viruses which infect bacteria. This was important in the early development of molecular biology. Delbrück was born in Berlin, German Empire. Trained as a physicist, he got his Ph.D. in 1930. he traveled through England, Denmark, and Switzerland. He met Wolfgang Pauli and Niels Bohr, who got him interested in biology. In 1937, he moved to the United States to pursue his interests in biology, taking up research in the Biology Division at Caltech on genetics of the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. While at Caltech Delbrück became acquainted with bacteria and their viruses (bacteriophage or 'phage'). Delbrück remained in the US during World War II, teaching physics at Vanderbilt University in Nashville while pursuing his genetic research. In 1942, he and Salvador Luria of Indiana University demonstrated that bacterial resistance to virus infection is caused by random mutation and not adaptive change. This research, known as the Luria-Delbrück experiment, was also significant for its use of mathematics to make quantitative predictions for the results to be expected from alternative models. For that work, they were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1969, sharing it with Alfred Hershey. During the 1940s Delbrück developed a course in bacteriophage genetics at the Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory to encourage interest in the field. In 1947, Delbrück returned to Caltech as a professor of biology where he remained until 1977.

Max Ernst (2 April 1891 – 1 April 1976) was a German painter and graphical artist. In 1919, he brought the art movement Dadaism to Germany, together with Johannes Theodor Baargeld. In 1922, he left Germany and moved to Paris, where he joined a group of Surrealists (a related art movement) led by André Breton. In 1941 he emigrated to the United States. He returned to France in 1953. With his paintings, collages, and sculptures, he created mysterious combinations using different ways of making images. Often he showed birds, and in landscapes that mimic a forest. He also wrote poems, and wrote about art. He was the first to use the techniques called Frottage and Grattage in art, which involve rubbing the canvas.

Maxwell Frank "Max" Clifford (6 April 1943 – 10 December 2017) was a British publicist and sex offender. Clifford was born in Kingston upon Thames and raised in Wimbledon. He left school when he was 15. Clifford was married to Elizabeth Porter from 1967 until her death in 2003. He has a daughter by her. He married Jo Westwood in 2010. She began divorce proceedings against him in August 2013 on the grounds of unreasonable behaviour. A decree nisi was granted in May 2014. He lived in Hersham before being sent to prison. He was arrested in December 2012 by Metropolitan Police officers as part of Operation Yewtree an investigation which was set up to investigate child sexual abuse committed by DJ Jimmy Savile who died in 2011, and by other people. In 2014, he was tried at Southwark Crown Court for 11 counts of indecent assault against teenage girls. On 28 April 2014 he was convicted of 8 counts. On 2 May 2014, he was sentenced to 8 years imprisonment and then incarcerated at HM Prison Littlehey in Cambridgeshire. He collapsed in his cell and was taken to hospital, where he died of a heart attack.

Max Horkheimer (February 14, 1895 – July 7, 1973) was a German-American philosopher and sociologist. He was famous for his work in critical theory as a member of the "Frankfurt School" of social research. His most important writing includes The Eclipse of Reason (1947), "Between Philosophy and Social Science" (1930–1938) and, together with Theodor Adorno, The Dialectic of Enlightenment (1947). Through the Frankfurt School, Horkheimer planned, supported, and made other significant works possible. After Hitler became Chancellor of Germany, Horkheimer, who was Jewish, left Germany and went to live in the United States. His collected works have been issued in German as Gesammelte Schriften, 19 volumes, edited by Alfred Schmidt and Gunzelin Schmid Noerr. S. Fischer Verlag, Frankfurt am Main 1985-1996.

The Max Headroom broadcast signal intrusion was a television signal hijacking that happened in Chicago, Illinois, United States, on the evening of November 22, 1987. It involved at least three unknown people. It is an example of what is known in the television business as broadcast signal intrusion. Two Chicago television stations, WGN-TV and WTTW, had their broadcast signals hijacked by an unknown person wearing a Max Headroom mask and sunglasses. A homemade Max Headroom background rocked back and forth in the background. The incident happened two times within a course of three hours. The first incident took place for 25 seconds during the sportscast on the 9:00 PM news on WGN-TV Channel 9, and the second, two hours later, after 11:00 PM on PBS related WTTW Channel 11 for about 90 seconds during a broadcast of an episode of the Doctor Who serial Horror of Fang Rock. The incident made national headlines and the people responsible have never been identified.

Max Kay (1936 – 5 June 2019) was a Scottish-born Australian entertainer and businessman. He started his career in Scotland and toured internationally as the manager of Andy Stewart. He lived in Perth, Western Australia from the 1960s onward. He performed as an entertainer in Perth. He also served as a councillor for the City of Perth. He received the Medal of the Order of Australia (OAM) in 2003 for services to entertainment. Kay died of pneumonia caused by cancer on 5 June 2019, at the age of 82.

Max Keith was a German businessman who invented Fanta during World War II in Germany. When he was 30 years old, he worked at a German subsidiary of Coca-Cola in 1933. Sales of Coca-Cola in Germany rose from 100,000 cases in 1933 to over 4 million cases in 1939. Because of the Allied blockade, Coca-Cola GmbH was unable to get Coca-Cola syrup during World War II. The supply of regular Coca-Cola ran out in 1942. To keep the plant in operation, Keith developed a fruit flavored drink made from apple fiber, left over from cider pressings, and whey, a byproduct from cheese manufacture, creating Fanta. Fanta sold three million cases in 1943, sustaining the firm's business in Germany. In 1945, at the last stages of the war, Keith was ordered by a German general to rename the subsidiary, but he refused. The general was killed in an air raid before any action was taken against Keith.

Sir Max Hugh Macdonald Hastings (; born 28 December 1945) is a British journalist. He has worked as a foreign correspondent for the BBC, editor-in-chief of The Daily Telegraph, and editor of the Evening Standard. He was born in London.

Maximilian Carl Emil Weber (pronounced: maks ˈveːbɐ) (21 April 1864 – 14 June 1920) was a German political economist and sociologist who was considered one of the founders of the modern study of sociology and public administration. He began his career at the University of Berlin, and later worked at Freiburg University, University of Heidelberg, University of Vienna and University of Munich. He had influence on German politics of his time, because he was an advisor to Germany's negotiators at the Treaty of Versailles and to the commission that drafted the Weimar Constitution. Weber is known for his work in the sociology of religion. His most famous work is his essay The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism. He disagreed with Karl Marx's view that class structure was the way to view how society worked. He believed that human values affected how people acted throughout history.

Max Rostal (born Cieszyn, 7 August 1905; died Bern, 6 August 1991) was a violinist who was a famous violin teacher. He was Austrian-born, but later took British citizenship. He was born in Cieszyn and studied with Carl Flesch. From 1930 to 1933 he taught at the Berlin Hochschule, from 1944 to 1958 at the Guildhall School of Music, London and then at the conservatory in Bern, Switzerland. Many of his pupils became famous players. They include three members of the Amadeus Quartet. Rostal played a wide variety of music, including many newly composed works such as Violin Concerto no 2 by Béla Bartók. He arranged the cadenza that Beethoven wrote for the piano version of his violin concerto ( for piano and timpani) for violin and timpani. He died in Bern.

Max Theiler (January 30, 1899 – August 11, 1972) was an South African-American virologist. He won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1951 for developing a vaccine against yellow fever. He was born on January 30, 1899 in Pretoria, South African Republic and died on August 11, 1972 in New Haven, Connecticut.

Max Ferdinand Perutz FRS OM CBE (19 May 1914 – 6 February 2002) was an Austrian-born British molecular biologist. He shared the 1962 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with John Kendrew, for their studies of the structures of haemoglobin and globular proteins. The method used was mainly X-ray crystallography. He went on to win the Royal Medal of the Royal Society in 1971 and the Copley Medal in 1979. At Cambridge he founded and chaired (1962–79) The Medical Research Council Laboratory of Molecular Biology, fourteen of whose scientists have won Nobel Prizes. Perutz's contributions to molecular biology in Cambridge are documented in The History of the University of Cambridge: Volume 4 (1870 to 1990) published by the Cambridge University Press in 1992. Perutz was born in Vienna, Austria. His family was Jewish. He had worked in Cambridge (Peterhouse College) since 1936, and moved to Britain permanently after the Anschluss, the Nazi takeover of Austria. He did his war work in Canada, and returned to Cambridge after the war. Max did some of his most important work after winning the Nobel award, and is still held in the highest esteem. 1989. Is science necessary? Essays on science and scientists. London. Barrie and Jenkins. 1997. Science is not a quiet life: unravelling the atomic mechanism of haemoglobin. Singapore. World Scientific. 2002. I wish I’d made you angry earlier: essays on science, scientists and humanity. Cold Spring Harbor, New York. Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press.

Juan Máximo Rojas Proenza, known as Max Rojas (June 4, 1940 - April 24, 2015) was a Mexican poet, essayist, literary critic and culture manager. Rojas wrote long-winded poem Cuerpos, his last published work originally composed of three thousand pages and that could fill twenty volumes.

Max Lüscher (September 9, 1923 – February 2, 2017) was a Swiss psychotherapist. He was known for inventing the Lüscher color test. This was a tool for measuring an individual's psycho-physical state based on his or her color preferences. Lüscher worked for international companies, among other things giving color advice. His book The Lüscher Test has been translated into more than 30 languages. Lüscher died in Lucerne, Switzerland on February 2, 2017, aged 93.

Maxwell Herman Alexander "Max" Newman, FRS (7 February 1897 – 22 February 1984) was a British mathematician and codebreaker. He was Jewish. He started the Royal Society Computing Machine Laboratory at the University of Manchester. This laboratory made the first working modern computer. The computer stored programs in 1948. This computer was called the Manchester Small-Scale Experimental Machine.

Max Osceola Jr. (August 13, 1950 – October 8, 2020) was a leader of the Native American Seminole Tribe of Florida. Osceola was an elected representative on the Seminole Tribal Council from 1985 through 2010. The South Florida Sun-Sentinel called Mr. Osceola “one of the tribe’s longest-serving and most powerful politicians.” He died on October 8, 2020 of COVID-19 at the age of 70.

Maxwell "Max" William Ward, (22 November 1921 – 2 November 2020) was a Canadian aviator. He was the founder of Wardair Airlines, at one time, the third-largest air carrier in Canada. Ward died on 2 November 2020 in Edmonton, Alberta at the age of 98.

Max Park (born November 28, 2001) is an American solver of the Rubik's Cube. As of September 24, 2022, he holds the world record for solving five cubes in a row. His fastest average time is 4.86 seconds per cube.and he has a world record with a time of 3.13 seconds

Max Moszkowicz Sr. (5 October 1926 – 27 January 2022) was a Dutch lawyer. The Jewish Moszkowicz family fled Nazi Germany in 1933. During the Holocaust his parents were murdered. Moszkowicz survived Auschwitz. He became well known in the Netherlands for defending Dutch criminals. Moszkowicz was a member of the People's Party for Freedom and Democracy (VVD). Moszkowicz died on 27 January 2022, at the age of 95.

Max Mercury is a fictional character from the DC Comics universe. The character was created by Jack Cole and Chuck Mazoujian, first appearing in National Comics #5 (1940). He is a legendary speedster who has traveled through time studying the Speed Force. Born in the 19th Century, he has taken different identities throughout history to fight crime. In his old age he becomes a mentor to other heroes, taking the reckless Impulse as his student. His other aliases have included Windrunner, Whip Whirlwind, Lightning and Quicksilver. In the Flashpoint Timeline, his real name is Maxwell Crandall. He has been a member of the All-Star Squadron, the Flash Family and the Freedom Fighters. Max Mercury appears in the 2014 to 2023 television series The Flash, portrayed by Trevor Carroll.

Max Stirner (1806–1856) was a German philosopher. His real name was Johann Caspar Schmidt. He was part of the world of the Young Hegelians. They were a group of young German thinkers. At first, they followed the philosopher Hegel. Later, they turned against many of his ideas. Stirner wrote only one important book. Its German title is Der Einzige und sein Eigentum (1844). This means "The Unique One and His Property". The best-known English title is The Ego and Its Own. In this book, Stirner follows one idea as far as he can. This idea is a criticism of what philosophers call alienation. Here, alienation means this: people take something that really comes from themselves. They turn it into a great idea above them. Then they obey it, as if it were their master. The Young Hegelians had already begun this kind of criticism. Stirner wanted to push it to the end. Stirner says that almost all Western thought makes the same mistake again and again. Christianity does this. So do idealism, belief in "Man", liberal politics, and modern socialism. Idealism is the belief that mind and ideas, not matter, are the deepest part of reality. Stirner says that each of these systems puts a general idea above the real, single person. These general ideas include God, Man, the State, Society, Morality, and Law. Here, words such as "the State" or "Society" do not name real, living things. They name general ideas. Each idea is treated as holy. The real person is then told to obey it. Against all these ideas, Stirner sets der Einzige, "the Unique One". By this, he means the living person, with a body, who cannot be reduced to any general idea. When the book appeared, several writers attacked it at once. They included Ludwig Feuerbach, Moses Hess, and a writer called Szeliga, who wrote for Bruno Bauer. Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels also wrote a long answer in their book The German Ideology. After this first debate, Stirner's book was almost forgotten. People found it again in the 1880s. Since then, it has been read in several ways. Some readers see it as one of the last works of the Young Hegelian movement. Some see it as part of the background to Marx's thought. Some see it as an early form of individualist anarchism. Some see it as close to Nietzsche, though probably not as a source for Nietzsche's ideas. In the 20th century, some readers also saw it as an early voice for some existentialist and later ideas. Johann Caspar Schmidt was born on 25 October 1806 in Bayreuth, a town in Germany. His family was Protestant and poor. His father made flutes. His father died six months after the boy was born. Two years later, his mother married again. Her new husband worked as an assistant in a pharmacy. The family moved to Kulm, in West Prussia. The boy spent his early years there. In 1818, the boy was sent back to Bayreuth. He lived with his godfather and went to school there. He completed the town's classical secondary school, called the Gymnasium. The head of the school was Georg Andreas Gabler. Years later, Gabler took Hegel's teaching post in philosophy in Berlin. At school, the other boys gave Schmidt the nickname "Stirner". The German word Stirn means "forehead". The boys chose this name because his forehead was high and large. The nickname stayed with him. Later, he used it as his pen name, that is, his author name. In 1826, Stirner began to study at the University of Berlin. He studied there for four terms. In Berlin, he came into direct contact with Hegel's philosophy. He went to three lecture courses given by Hegel himself. One was on the philosophy of religion, in the summer of 1827. One was on the history of philosophy. One was on the philosophy of mind, or "spirit". He also went to lectures by other well-known teachers. Schleiermacher taught ethics. Neander taught the history of the Church. Marheineke taught Christian doctrine. Later writers say that Stirner knew Hegel's main books well. This can be seen in the way The Unique One uses them. After Berlin, Stirner went to Erlangen in 1828. There he took courses from Christian Kapp, a Hegelian teacher. Then, in 1829, he went to Königsberg. After that, there was a long break in his studies. This break was probably caused by his mother's growing mental illness. In 1832, he came back to Berlin to finish his degree. Stirner had to pass a state exam to become a teacher. This exam was called the Staatsexamen. He took it in 1834 and 1835, but it did not go well. The main man who tested him was Friedrich Adolf Trendelenburg. Trendelenburg followed the ideas of Aristotle. He did not like Hegel's logic, and he said so openly. For this reason, Trendelenburg gave Stirner only a limited right to teach. With this right, Stirner could teach. But he could not get a regular, permanent teaching job. So Stirner gave up the hope of working at a university. In 1835 and 1836 he worked at a school in Berlin, but he was not paid for it. In December 1837 he got married. His wife was Agnes Clara Kunigunde Butz. She was the daughter of his landlady (the woman he rented his room from). His young wife died in August 1838. She died while she was giving birth to a baby. The baby was also dead when it was born. In October 1839 Stirner at last found a job with pay. He taught at a private school for girls. A woman called Madame Gropius ran this school. Stirner taught literature and history at this school for five years. He kept the job almost until his book came out. From late 1841, Stirner often spent time with a group called "the Free Ones" (die Freien). They were young Hegelians who lived in Berlin. They met in a wine bar called Hippel's, on a street called the Friedrichstraße. The most important thinker in the group was Bruno Bauer. Other people in the group were Edgar and Egbert Bauer, Ludwig Buhl, Eduard Meyen, and Arnold Ruge. Karl Marx was part of the same world of young Hegelians. He also knew Bauer's circle of friends. But it is not clear how much Marx really took part in this group. It is also not clear how well he knew Stirner. More is known about Stirner's link with Friedrich Engels. Engels knew Stirner in person. Engels even drew the only picture of Stirner that still exists. He did not look at Stirner while he drew it. He drew the picture from memory, in London, in 1892. In some of his letters, Engels says that he and Stirner often talked about Hegel's way of thinking (his dialectic). In 1841 and 1842, Stirner also went to a class about Hegel's Logic (one of Hegel's books). A teacher called Karl Werder gave this class. Other people who went to it were Engels, Bakunin, Kierkegaard, and the writer Turgenev. One scholar points out that, overall, Stirner had studied Hegel at least as much as most of the other young Hegelians had. Before he wrote his big book, Stirner wrote several articles for left-wing magazines. He wrote a review of a short book by Bruno Bauer, printed without the author's name (January 1842). He wrote a long essay on education, Das unwahre Prinzip unserer Erziehung ("The False Principle of Our Education", April 1842). He wrote a study called Kunst und Religion ("Art and Religion", June 1842). He also wrote about the idea of a state based on love (1843). He reviewed a novel by Eugène Sue, The Mysteries of Paris (1843). On 21 October 1843 he married for the second time. His new wife was Marie Wilhelmine Dähnhardt (1818–1902). She was a free young woman from Gadebusch. She also visited the Free Ones, and she had inherited much money. The wedding was strange and playful. Bruno Bauer was a witness. The wedding rings were made there and then from copper taken from his purse. This is one of the few stories that we still have about Stirner's life. The Unique One and His Property (Der Einzige und sein Eigentum) came out in Leipzig at the start of November 1844. The title page gave the date 1845. The first printing had one thousand copies. The authorities in Leipzig took two hundred and fifty of them. But the Saxon minister of the interior soon ended the ban. He said that the book was "too absurd" to be dangerous. The book quickly caused a sharp argument. Szeliga (for Bauer), Moses Hess, and Feuerbach each printed an answer against it. Marx and Engels wrote The German Ideology, a long manuscript that was not printed until 1932. In it they spend almost three quarters of the book attacking Stirner. They make fun of him by calling him "Saint Max". Stirner answered his critics in September 1845 in a piece called Rezensenten Stirners ("Stirner's Critics"). In 1847 he answered the philosopher Kuno Fischer in another piece, signed with the clear pen name "G. Edward". The first excitement was strong but short. Stirner left his teaching job just before the book came out. In 1845 he tried to run a business selling milk in the suburbs of Berlin. The business failed and used up his wife's money. Marie Dähnhardt left him at the end of 1846, and they divorced in 1850. Now poor, Stirner kept himself alive by translating into German the works on economics of Jean-Baptiste Say (1845–1846) and Adam Smith (1846–1847). This made eight volumes of honest work, but without the translator's notes that he had promised. His last book was a History of the Reaction (1852). It was little more than a set of extracts from Burke, Comte, and other conservative writers. Stirner went to prison twice for debt (1853 and 1854). In May 1856, in his rooms on the Philippstraße, a poisonous insect stung him on the neck. He died on 25 June from the blood poisoning that followed. Bruno Bauer and Ludwig Buhl were among the few people at his funeral. Stirner's work is easiest to understand when we know its background. This background is the break-up of Hegel's school in Germany in the 1830s and 1840s. Hegel had died in 1831. After his death, his followers split into two groups. The right wing was led by Marheineke and Gabler. It kept Hegel's system close to Christianity. It also defended the power of the rational state. The left wing used Hegel's method against Hegel's own conclusions. David Friedrich Strauss, in his Life of Jesus (1835), treated the Gospel stories as myths. Bruno Bauer went further. He made self-consciousness, that is, the mind that knows itself, the only true starting point of philosophy. Ludwig Feuerbach, in The Essence of Christianity (1841), changed the study of religion into the study of human nature. For Feuerbach, God is only an image that human beings make of their own nature. People take their own shared nature, put it in the sky, call it God, and then feel small before it. Feuerbach called this shared human nature the "species-being" (Gattungswesen). Stirner wrote his book above all against Feuerbach. Feuerbach thought that he had completed the criticism of religion. Stirner says that he had not. By putting "Man" in the place of God, Feuerbach did not end the holy. He only moved it. Feuerbach's "humanity" became a new idol. It stands above the single, real person and tells that person to bow down. So it does the same work as the old God. This leads to the main claim of The Unique One and His Property. The claim is this: the whole tradition of philosophy keeps making one move. From Christianity to liberalism and socialism, through idealism and godless humanism, thinkers keep raising some general idea above the single person. The idea may be God, Spirit, Man, Society, Humanity, Morality, or Law. Then they tell the single person to serve it. Stirner sums this up in a famous line. He says that the newest rebellions against God are only theological insurrections. (Theological means "to do with God and religion".) In other words, even the people who fight God still think in the old religious way. Stirner's link to Hegel has been read in opposite ways. Henri Arvon, in a book of 1954, saw The Unique One as the logical end of Hegel's philosophy. Others read it as a plain, mocking rejection of Hegel's method. Newer research suggests a more careful answer. Lawrence Stepelevich calls Stirner the "true heir" of Hegel. In his view Stirner stands at the closing point of Hegel's great circle of thought. Jeff Spiessens reads the book as a "departure" from Hegel made with Hegel's own tools. Stirner takes over Hegel's language and logic and treats them as his own property. He uses them to turn around the link between the thinker and his thoughts. In Hegel's system the single person gets his meaning from the growth of Spirit. Stirner puts the single, real person back in charge, as the owner of his thoughts and the maker of his ideas. The book opens and closes with the same line. The line comes from a poem by Goethe (Vanitas! Vanitatum vanitas!, 1806). In German it is Ich hab' Mein' Sach' auf Nichts gestellt. The French translator R. L. Reclaire put it as "I have based my cause on nothing." This repeated line frames the whole work. The book returns to its starting point after passing through everything in between. The book has two parts. The split between them copies the break that Stirner is trying to make. The first part is called "Man" (Der Mensch). It tells the history of the chains that have been put on the single person, both in real history and in philosophy. The second part is called "I" (Ich). It sets out Stirner's own position. Each of the two parts divides into three. Because of this, the book has a shape that is strangely close to Hegel's own model, even though its content claims to reject that model. The second part moves through three steps: Eigenheit (ownness, being one's own; Reclaire calls it "property"), Der Eigner (the owner), and Der Einzige (the Unique One). The middle chapter again divides into three: Meine Macht (my power), Mein Verkehr (my dealings with others), and Mein Selbstgenuß (my enjoyment of myself). The first part opens with a chapter called "A Human Life" (Ein Menschenleben). This chapter matters more than it may seem. It gives a pattern of three ages: childhood, youth, and grown adulthood. This pattern shapes the whole book. It is also a clear re-use, and twist, of Hegel's own account of the ages of life. The child lives in a "realist" way. The child is ruled by things, by a strict father, and by the stick. This lasts until the child finds its own cleverness and inner life. The young person then discovers "the mind" or "spirit" (Geist) and enters an "idealist" stage. The young person breaks free from the outside world. But now the young person becomes a servant to his own ideas, his beliefs, and his conscience. Only the grown adult, the egoist, reaches the place where neither things nor ideas rule any more. The adult holds power over both. The second chapter is "The Ancients and the Moderns" (Menschen der alten und der neuen Zeit). It moves the same pattern onto world history. The Ancients are the world before Christianity, both Greeks and Romans. They match the childhood of mankind. They are "realists" who fight a world that pushes back. Christianity opens the modern age and the youth of mankind. It teaches that the real enemy is no longer the outside world but the inner self: the passions, the "old Adam". So the Christian fight is the fight of spirit against flesh. The Moderns are the Christians and those who came after them. They live in a "world of ghosts" (Gespenster). In this world unseen ideas hold the single person more tightly than nature ever did. Two ideas stand at the heart of Stirner's criticism: the "phantom" (Spuk or Gespenst) and the "fixed idea" (fixe Idee). A phantom is any general idea that is raised into a holy power above the single person, so that the person must kneel before it. Such ideas include God, Man, Freedom, Justice, Law, Morality, Society, and Humanity. God was the chief phantom of the Christian age. But, for Stirner, the modern, godless words are only more hidden phantoms that do exactly the same work. Reason, Spirit, Humanity, Society, History: all of these still rule the person from above. A "fixed idea" is an idea that owns a person without the person knowing it. It is a belief that has taken hold so deeply that the person can no longer separate himself from it. Stirner says the right link to thought is the other way round. A person should own his ideas. He should not be owned by them. Stirner's most surprising claim is about the modern age. Modern philosophy did not free people from Christianity, he says. It only carried Christianity further. Luther's Reformation made religion more inward, and so it gave spirit an even firmer grip on the person. The Enlightenment put Reason in the place of God, but it left the power of Reason just as large. German idealism made the world fully spiritual, with Spirit as the very ground of what is real. And when Feuerbach says that the secret of religion is human nature, he only swaps one phantom for another. He puts "Man" where God used to be. Modern humanism, Stirner says, is a religion that has changed its object but not its shape. Stirner spreads this criticism across the whole politics of his time. He sorts the politics of freedom, called liberalism, into three kinds. The first is political liberalism. It was born from the French Revolution. It declares that all citizens are free and equal. But this freedom is only on paper. By making the State the one ruling power, it ties the person to the citizen, and the citizen to the State. The second is social liberalism, that is, the socialism and communism of his day. It tries to fix the gaps in political liberalism by ending private property. But it only puts Society in the place of the State as the new ruler. Now the person must obey the group and shape his life to fit the needs of social work. The third is human, or humanitarian, liberalism. This is the kind held by Feuerbach and Bruno Bauer. It wants to free man by stripping away everything special about him, such as his religion, his nation, and his social place. It keeps only his bare humanity. For Stirner this is the deepest loss of all. It asks the person to be nothing but "a human being", a sample of the species. In doing so, it takes away everything that makes the person this one, single person. Next to the split between Ancients and Moderns, Stirner uses a second map of history. This second map shows his link to Hegel clearly. It rests on a way of sorting human "races" that Hegel had set out in his Encyclopaedia (section 393). This was a racist scheme, and it ranked the so-called races in order. Stirner takes it over. He speaks of a "Negro" age, a "Mongol" age, and a "Caucasian" age. He writes that "the history of mankind is really only the history of the Caucasian race." This passage is racist. It also puts Europe at the centre of history. Stirner took this way of thinking from Hegel. Stirner treats these "ages" as stages of the spirit rather than as fixed facts of biology. So it is not racism in the strict biological sense. But it is still plainly racist, and it puts Europe at the centre. Stirner then uses the same scheme inside European history. He calls the "Negro" stage the time when people depend on the world of the senses and on nature. He ties this to the ancient world. He calls the "Mongol" stage the time when people obey custom and the spirit fixed in laws and institutions. He ties this to the Christian age. The last stage is the rise of a person's own selfhood, which would let him master both of the others. As Spiessens shows, Stirner uses Hegel's philosophy of history in order to turn its meaning upside down. Hegel had described history as the slow growth of the awareness of freedom. Stirner reads the same history as the growing slavery of the person to ideas that press on him harder and harder. The second part of the book, called simply "I", sets out Stirner's own position. Its central idea is "the Unique One" (der Einzige). But the Unique One is not a concept (a general idea) in the usual sense. Stirner writes that, of "Me" as of God, no concept can express him; nothing that people give as his essence (the fixed inner nature a thing is supposed to have) catches all of him; these are only names. The Unique One is not an essence, not a type of person, and not a quality shared by all people. It is the single, real person, just as that person cannot be put under any heading. The Unique One is, in Stirner's phrase, "the creative Nothing, the Nothing out of which I myself make everything." The book's founding line, "I have based my cause on nothing", now becomes clear. The single person has not based his cause on God, or on Man, or on Truth, or on any idea given in advance. He has based it on himself, as a "nothing" with respect to every essence one might name. So the Unique One is sharply different from Feuerbach's "Man", from the "Subject" of idealism, and from the "citizen" of liberal politics. All of these are general ideas. Each one claims to grasp what the person is deep down. So each one ties the person to a rule from outside. As Stirner writes near the end of the book, he is not one "self" beside other "selves"; he is the only self; he is Unique. Each person is a Unique One who cannot be compared with any other. This is not because the person has rare gifts. It is because his single existence goes beyond every idea. The Unique One is neither good nor bad, neither free nor enslaved, neither selfish nor giving in the moral sense of these words. He is the one who stands on himself as his own ground, and who allows no power above him the right to judge him. One of the book's main joints is the difference between freedom (Freiheit) and ownness (Eigenheit; Reclaire renders it as "property"). Freedom, as modern political and philosophical movements ask for it, is mostly a "no" word. It means the lack of outside chains, the escape from a master. But, Stirner notes, freedom of this kind is a wish that never ends. Once a person is free of one master, he finds another. When old kinds of rule are pulled down, new ones go up. More deeply, freedom always depends on the very thing it wants to be free from. It is Befreiung, a process of getting free, and so it stays tied to its enemy. Ownness works the other way. It is not a state to reach but a power to use. The German word is hard to put into English. It can be rendered as "ownness", "selfhood", or "being one's own". It joins three ideas: what is one's own (eigen), having oneself, and being one single, unrepeatable person. Freedom always hangs on outside conditions. Ownness hangs only on the person himself. It is not a far-off goal to chase. It is a strength to put to work. So Stirner changes the basic question. The question is no longer "Am I free?" but "Do I own myself?" A person does not win this self-ownership through political revolutions or social reforms. He wins it through a practical taking-back of himself, an act that frees him from being ruled. This act changes both his inner attitude and his behaviour towards the State, the law, the institutions, and his promises. The difference between revolution (Revolution) and insurrection (Empörung, "a rising up", sometimes also put as "revolt") cannot be split from the last one. Stirner states it in plain words. He says that revolution and insurrection are not the same. A revolution overturns the standing order, the set-up of the State or of Society. So it has only a political or social meaning. An insurrection does lead, as a side effect, to the same overturning of standing institutions. But that is not its aim. It grows only out of people's discontent. It is not a taking-up of arms. It is the act of single people who rise, who stand up straight. A revolution aims at a new order. An insurrection leads people to stop letting themselves be ruled, and to rule themselves instead. A revolution tells people to build a new order. An insurrection tells them to rise and stand up. The point of this difference goes beyond politics. Every revolution, because it wants to set up a new order, stays caught in the logic of ruling. It swaps one master for another, one phantom for another. The French Revolution ended the monarchy only to set up the rule of the people and the power of the State. Socialist revolutions plan to end private property only to set up shared property. In both cases the single person stays under a power above him. An insurrection is different. Its aim is not to change the standing order. Its aim is to assert the person against the order, whatever the order is. It is not a group rising in the name of some higher ideal. It is the act by which the person stops recognising any power above him. Stirner's idea of property (Eigentum) is not the same as the legal "private property" that the liberals defend. It is also not the same as the property the socialists attack. It grows out of ownness. For Stirner, property is everything that the person can take and hold by his own power. He writes that what he can get hold of, he seizes and makes his own. What gets away from him, he has no right to. He does not boast of any "rights" he might claim over it, and he takes no comfort in them. So Stirner rejects two things at once. He rejects property guaranteed by law, which he sees as only a legal phantom. He also rejects the socialist attack on private property, which only hands the same job to "society", a new holy thing. "My property", he writes, "is what is in my power." This idea goes past money and goods. Thoughts too can become a person's property. Or, and this is the mark of the enslaved person, the person can be owned by his thoughts. The religious man is owned by the idea of God. The moral man is owned by the idea of the Good. The patriot is owned by the idea of the nation. Each time, an idea has seized the person, instead of the person seizing the idea. The Unique One does the opposite. He owns his ideas instead of being owned by them. He uses them as tools that serve his enjoyment and his power. Thought stops being a holy calling and becomes a tool. Stirner's attack on morals is one of the central parts of the book. He throws out the whole moral vocabulary, such as duty, obligation, virtue, right, sin, and the sacred. He sees these words as leftovers from religion. Moral thinking always has the same shape, he says, whether it comes from religion, from Kant, or from humanism. It sets up a rule outside the person. The rule may be a command from God, Kant's "categorical imperative" (his supreme moral law), or the demand of human nature. Then it orders the person to obey. Every "you shall" (du sollst), Stirner says, is a holy command. It claims a power over the person that the person never agreed to. Against morals Stirner sets what he calls conscious egoism. But Stirner's egoism has little to do with common selfishness, the simple chase after money or pleasure. The egoist, in Stirner's sense, is not always the person who wants riches or low pleasure. He is the person who knows no measure but himself. He makes his own enjoyment and power the only test of what he does. Such an egoist can still be kind, caring, and ready to help others. He does these things not because he "must", but because he "wants" to, because it pleases him, because it serves his enjoyment. The difference between morals and egoism is not in what people do. It is in why they do it. In the first case the person acts from duty, under an outside rule. In the second case the person acts from enjoyment of himself (Selbstgenuß), as the owner of his own deeds. As the writer Saul Newman notes, Stirner's egoism is less a teaching about self-interest than a form of ruling oneself and being master of oneself. Stirner's stand against religion goes past plain atheism. The Young Hegelians worked to show that God does not exist, that religion is a false belief, and that the holy must dissolve into the everyday. Stirner agrees with this, but he thinks it does not go far enough. The atheist attack on religion, he says, stays caught in the holy. This is because it sets up new absolutes, such as Reason, Man, Science, and Society. These do the same job as the old God. Feuerbach's atheism is a religion turned inside out. Humanism is a religion that has changed its object but not its shape. So Stirner attacks not only God but the holy as such. He attacks everything that claims to stand above the person and to ask from him respect, worship, or sacrifice. In another famous phrase of Stirner, Feuerbach's criticism is only a "theological insurrection": a rising-up against the old god that ends by setting up a new one. Stirner's attack on the State cannot be split from his attack on law. The State, in any form, is always a power that sets itself above people and forces its will on them by strength and by law. This is true of a kingdom, a democracy, or a socialist state. Law (Recht, also "right") is, for Stirner, only a will that is foreign to the person but that the person is told to obey. Natural law, human rights, written law: all are forms of one trick. They all claim that certain rules bind the person whatever he wills and whatever power he has. For Stirner, the only real ground of any power is the actual strength of the one who uses it. He writes that force is himself, the one who is powerful, the one who holds the power. Law, he says, is only the power of others, dressed up as a holy rule and called "right". The "others" are the State, society, or the ruling class. This leads Stirner to reject every kind of political order built on law. He rejects the liberal State, which guarantees freedoms on paper at the price of obeying the law. He rejects the socialist State, which plans to guarantee material equality at the price of obeying society. More deeply, he rejects the very idea of society (Gesellschaft) as a thing with a being and a power of its own. Society, as modern political thinkers picture it, is a new phantom. It does not exist apart from the people who make it up. Yet it claims to rule over them. Against all these forms of grouping, Stirner sets what he calls the union of egoists (Verein von Egoisten). The union is sharply different from society and the State. It rests on no principle, no goal, and no contract that would give it a being apart from its members. Reclaire, in a translator's note, points out that the German Verein means an active, willing working-together, while Gesellschaft means a passive grouping forced on its members. The union is a freely chosen link between people who join to serve their own interests. They can break the link at any time, once it no longer suits them. It has no constitution, no laws, no rights. It does not own its members; its members own it. In society the person is a means that serves the whole. In the union the whole is a means that serves the persons. Stirner adds that the person must always be "more than" the union. If the union ever swallowed him, it would itself turn into a phantom. The union of egoists is not a political programme in the usual sense. Stirner does not offer a model of a new kind of group to replace the present institutions. The union is, first of all, a way of describing a kind of link between Unique Ones. It is a link of power and enjoyment, built not on law or duty but on interest and desire. The Unique One joins with other Unique Ones not because a contract or a command forces him, but because the link adds to his enjoyment. As soon as it stops serving him, he leaves it. So the union does not have to last. It can end when its members no longer want it. It is the opposite of society, which wants to be lasting and binding. In The German Ideology, Marx saw this union as just a copy, in ideas, of middle-class civil society. Later writers have often found this reading too simple, since Stirner's union does not fit neatly into the liberal picture of a contract. Stirner puts great weight on the body and on the matter of the single person. This plays a large part in his fight against idealist ideas. Again and again he brings the person back to his real, dying, feeling existence, against the essences that the tradition wants to give him. He does not build a full philosophy of the body, like the ones later worked out by Feuerbach, Nietzsche, or Merleau-Ponty. For Stirner the body works rather as a weapon in argument. It is the hard, real test on which the great moral and metaphysical ideas break. (Metaphysical means "having to do with the deepest nature of reality, beyond what the senses show".) In this sense he writes that, when the world stands in his way (and it always does), he consumes it to still the hunger of his egoism. The picture of eating comes back again and again. The person's link to the world is a link of eating, taking, and enjoyment. It is not a link of calm knowing or of spiritual sharing. This link between the body, eating, and self-enjoyment (Selbstgenuß) holds the book together. For Stirner enjoyment is not a calm looking-on, and it is not pleasure in the low sense. It is the active use of a power that feels itself in taking. It is the movement by which the person spreads out as he takes hold of the things, thoughts, and links that are open to him. The idealist tradition, from Plato to German idealism, makes thought a stepping-back from the world of the senses. It treats calm looking-on as the highest link to the world. Stirner turns this judgement around. Thought has worth only as a tool of the bodily person who uses it. The world has reality only as matter to be consumed. This prepares the last part of the book, Mein Selbstgenuß ("my enjoyment of myself"). There the egoist appears as the one who "uses himself up" as he spreads out, without saving himself for some higher cause that would justify him in advance. After the short flash of 1844–1846, The Unique One and His Property fell into almost complete forgetting. The Revolution of 1848 failed. Stirner took no part in it, and he had already condemned its liberal and social aims in advance. With the failure of 1848, the debates of the young Hegelians sank too. The ideas Stirner had fought against had themselves gone under. So interest in his book, which was mostly about those debates, faded. Only a few mentions of it remained. They appear in Erdmann (1866), in Lange's History of Materialism (1866), and in Eduard von Hartmann. The book was found again from 1888. The poet John Henry Mackay (a German in spite of his Scottish name) was caught by the title, which he had seen named in Lange. He spent ten years putting Stirner's life back together. He asked for witnesses in the newspapers. In 1898 he printed a life of Stirner that is still the main source for all later ones: Max Stirner. Sein Leben und sein Werk. One event helped to spread Stirner's name to the wider public. On 28 March 1892, after a performance of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony, the conductor Hans von Bülow said Stirner's name out loud in public and linked it to that of Bismarck. The rise of Nietzsche's philosophy at the same time led people to link the two men. But this link has been argued about ever since. From the late 19th century, many writers compared The Unique One with Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra. Yet there is no clear proof that one came from the other. One late and second-hand report says that Nietzsche told a student, Adolf Baumgartner, to read Stirner in 1874. Nietzsche had probably learned the name from Lange. But Nietzsche never names Stirner in his writings or his letters. The list of books he borrowed from the Basel library between 1869 and 1879 does not include the book. As Arvon concludes, there is no document that lets anyone say Stirner had an influence on Nietzsche. Stirner's afterlife runs along several lines. Individualist anarchism is one. In its American form, Benjamin Tucker brought out the first English translation in 1907, under the title The Ego and His Own. Tucker called it the most important book he had ever published. Anarchists of this kind claimed Stirner as a forerunner. Yet Stirner himself never accepted the label "anarchist", and his thought goes beyond the limits of any political programme. Paterson points to the gap between Stirner's egoism, which has no principles, and Tucker's moralised idea of a contract. Stirner's links with the great names of historical anarchism are slight at most. These names include Proudhon, Bakunin, Kropotkin, and Tolstoy. He shares with them only the stand against the State. His selfish individualism stays foreign to their social and ethical concerns. In the 20th century Stirner's thought fed several different readings. Henri Arvon, in his book of 1954, made Stirner a forerunner of French existentialism. Stirner puts existence before essence. He refuses any fixed human nature. He gives a central place to insurrection. All these points bring Stirner close to some themes in Sartre and Camus, even if no direct line can be proved. Later, some Situationist and "post-anarchist" readers brought Stirner's themes back to life. Saul Newman in particular sees Stirner as a forerunner of Michel Foucault's criticism of power, and of how people are shaped into subjects. Some recent writers read Stirner in another way. They say that he still belongs to the world of Hegel's philosophy. They show that his ideas, such as the Unique One, ownness, insurrection, and the union, get their real meaning only when read against the dialectic that they both use and turn around. For a long time Stirner stayed pushed to the side of the official history of philosophy. He was often cut down to the cartoon that Marx and Engels drew in The German Ideology. Today he looks like one of the end points of the break-up of Hegel's school. He is the one who pushes the criticism of alienation to its limit. He refuses to let any essence at all, even human nature, be the ground of the person. His thought stays a challenge to every kind of making-holy. The holy thing may be God, Man, Society, the Market, or any other power that claims to stand above the single, real person and to demand from him respect, obedience, or sacrifice.

Max Alfons Miedinger (December 24, 1910 – March 8, 1980) was a Swiss designer and typeface designer. He is best known for having designed the Helvetica typeface in 1957, together with Eduard Hoffmann.

Aleksei Maksimovich Peshkov (In Russian Алексей Максимович Пешков) (Old style: 16 March 1868, New style: 28 March – 18 June 1936), better known as Maxim Gorky (Максим Горький), was a Soviet/Russian author, a founder of the socialist realism literary method and a political activist. From 1906 to 1913 and from 1921 to 1929 he lived abroad, mostly in Capri, Italy; after his return to the Soviet Union he accepted the cultural policies of the time, although he was not permitted to leave the country.
Maximilian Franz Joseph Cornelius Wolf (21 June 1863 – 3 October 1932) was a German astronomer. He was born in Heidelberg, Germany. He discovered the first Trojan asteroid, 588 Achilles.

Maxim Sergeyevich Martsinkevich (, 8 May 1984 – 16 September 2020), better known as Tesak (Cleaver, Hatchet, Hand Axe, Machete), was a Russian neo-Nazi activist, media personality, vlogger, and the leader and co-founder of the Restruct movement. He was known for his white power skinhead and the leader of the far-right youth group Format 18. He was also a key member of Occupy Pedophilia. Martsinkevich received three prison sentences for inciting racial or ethnic hatred. Tesak was first indicted in 2007, after disrupting political debates by performing the Nazi salute and yelling "Sieg Heil!" at a book club in Moscow. In 2009, he was sentenced to three years for making a video with racist content. In the autumn of 2013, Tesak was indicted again for releasing new videos featuring racist remarks. As a result, on 15 August 2014, he was sentenced to five years in prison. On 11 November 2014, the court reduced the sentence to two years and 10 months. On 27 June 2017, the Babushkinsky district court of Moscow sentenced Martsinkevich to ten years in a strict regimen corrective labor colony for his involvement in attacks targeting synthetic cannabinoids dealers. He got killed in prison on 16 September 2020 at the age of 36.

Max van Rooy (25 March 1942 – 8 December 2022) was a Dutch writer and journalist. Van Rooy grew up in the region of The Hague where he attended primary school Passchalischool (1948-1954) and secondary school Aloysius College (1954-1961). He started studying cultural anthropology at the University of Amsterdam with professor André Köbben, but stopped after three months because he wanted to start writing and drawing. After school he had to do military service, and did that Royal Netherlands Air Force. After the end of his military service after two years Van Rooy chose to become an artist in Greece. Once back in the Netherlands, he settled in Amsterdam and became friends with writers K. Schippers, J. Bernlef and Gerard Brands.. Van Rooy was from 1966 to 1970 editor of newspaper Algemeen Handelsblad. Afterwards he was editor of the Saturday edition of NRC Handelsblad. In 1976 he became editor-in-chief of the cultural magazine Hollands Diep. In 1979 he returned to the NRC Handelsblad and became deputy editor-in-chief and architecture critic. In 1995 those positions changed to cultural commentator and architecture critic. He retired in 2010. Van Rooy was also writer and wrote multiple books. The last book he published was a biography about his grandfather architect Hendrik Petrus Berlage of the period until 1914. THe book shows he played a key role in the early 20th-century. With intervals it took him 44 years to write the book. van Rooy died in on 8 December 2022, at the age of 80.

Maximilian Kolbe (8 January 1894 – 14 August 1941) was a Polish Franciscan priest (Conventual Franciscan). He is known for volunteering to die in place of another prisoner, Franciszek Gajowniczek, at the Auschwitz concentration camp in 1941. Kolbe was born in Zduńska Wola, Poland (then part of the Russian Empire). He was baptized Raymund. He joined the Conventual Franciscans and was ordained a priest in 1918. In 1917, Kolbe helped to start the association Militia of the Immaculata (Militia Immaculatae) in Rome. He set up a large friary and printing house at Niepokalanów, near Warsaw, which printed the monthly magazine Rycerz Niepokalanej (Knight of the Immaculate). In 1930 he opened a mission house in Nagasaki, Japan, where a Japanese edition of the magazine (Seibo no Kishi) began to appear. In 1917 Kolbe started a Catholic group called the Immaculata Militia (Militia Immaculatae). Its members consecrate themselves to the Virgin Mary and try to bring other people to Jesus through her. Kolbe used printing, radio, and new monasteries, including one in Japan, to spread this movement. The group is still active in many countries today. During World War II, Kolbe was arrested by the German authorities and sent to Auschwitz. In July 1941 he offered to take the place of a prisoner chosen to die after an escape from the camp. After two weeks without food and water, he was killed on 14 August 1941 by a lethal injection. Kolbe was beatified on 17 October 1971 and canonized on 10 October 1982. His feast day is 14 August.

Maximilian Reinelt (24 August 1988 – 9 February 2019) was a German rower and physician. He won a gold medal at the 2012 Summer Olympics, and a silver medal at the 2016 Summer Olympics. He also won two World Championships and four European Championships. In 2016, he was awarded the Silbernes Lorbeerblatt, Germany's highest sports award. He was born in Ulm, West Germany. Reinelt died on 9 February 2019 during a skiing accident in St. Moritz, Switzerland, aged 30..

Maxine Kumin (June 6, 1925 – February 6, 2014) was an American poet and author. She became Poet Laureate Consultant in Poetry to the Library of Congress in 1981–1982. Kumin died on February 6, 2014 in Warner, New Hampshire. She was 88. Her death came after a year of bad health. She had a husband, Victor, and three children.

May-Britt Moser is a Norwegian psychologist and neuroscientist. Moser was born on Jan 4, 1962 in Fosnavåg, on a coastal island north of Bergen, Norway. She married Edvard Moser as a student of the University of Oslo in 1985. They had two kids, Isabel and Ailin. The Mosers were directors and coordinators of the Kavil Institute for systems Neuroscience and the Centre for Neural Computation at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology for many years, but they divorced in 2016. Each earned a PhD in neurobiology in 1995. She used rats as test subjects during her research because their nervous system is very similar to humans. They discovered brain cells that allow animals to move from one place to another. These are called grid cells, and they fire when the rats pass a certain location. Over time, this helped the rats move purposely around the room and navigate their surroundings. The Mosers won a Nobel Prize, an important award. She won this award in 2014 and shared this with John O’Keefe, another neuroscientist. They also won the Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize. She was elected a member of the Academia Europaea in 2011.

Maxwell Lord IV is a fictional character appearing in comic books published by DC Comics. The character first appeared in Justice League #1 (May 1987) and was created by Keith Giffen, J. M. DeMatteis, and Kevin Maguire. He is a powerful businessman. Maxwell Lord was important in the formation of the Justice League International in the DC Universe.
